The short answer is yes, you can absolutely put your Steam library on a NAS, but your network speed, drive choice, and protocol matter more than the box itself.
 Hosting games from network attached storage has become a real option now that 2.5GbE and 10GbE networking are cheap, and modern NAS hardware packs enough CPU power to handle the small file requests that game engines throw at storage. I ran Cyberpunk 2077, Baldur’s Gate 3, and Counter-Strike 2 from each of these devices to see which ones delivered playable load times and stable frame rates.

 The Synology DS225+ is the NAS I recommend to friends who want a low-friction entry into hosting Steam libraries. Synology’s DSM operating system makes it almost trivial to set up an SMB share, and Steam sees it as a standard network drive.
 I loaded my 2TB Steam library onto the DS225+ over a 2.5GbE connection, and load times for older games like Civilization VI and Total War: Warhammer III were within 10-15% of internal SSD speeds. Modern open-world games with constant asset streaming (think Starfield or Cyberpunk 2077) were playable but showed minor texture pop-in during fast camera movements.
 The Intel CPU inside handles concurrent streams without breaking a sweat, and the multi-layer data protection (RAID, snapshots, automated cloud backups) gives me peace of mind. I tested Steam downloads hitting the NAS at full gigabit-plus speeds while another user streamed 4K video from Plex, and neither suffered noticeable slowdowns.
 The biggest limitation is the lack of hardware video transcoding. If you only stream to your own devices, that does not matter, but remote Plex streaming at high bitrates will push the CPU hard. For a Steam library NAS that stays on your local network, the DS225+ punches well above its weight class.
 Steam library performance and RAID setup
 For Steam hosting, I configured RAID 1 with two 8TB drives, which mirrored my library and gave redundant protection. The DS225+ sustained around 280 MB/s sequential reads, which is more than enough for game loading over a 2.5GbE network connection. Random 4K reads hovered around 1,200 IOPS, and that is where modern open-world games start to feel sluggish on any NAS over network.
 The DSM interface lets you create the SMB share, set permissions, and map it as a Steam library folder in under 10 minutes. After that, Steam treats it like any other local drive. Installing and launching games from the network share worked without a single hiccup in my testing.
 Who should skip the DS225+
 If you have a 10GbE network and want to push every last megabyte through your switch, the DS225+ is not the right pick. It tops out at 2.5GbE and does not have a PCIe slot for upgrade. Power users running 20+ TB Steam libraries on SSD pools will also want a 4-bay unit with NVMe caching.
 Gamers who primarily play asset-streaming titles (Star Citizen, Microsoft Flight Simulator, Baldur’s Gate 3 with mods) will see better results from an SSD-based NAS or one with dedicated NVMe cache. The DS225+ is best for gamers who play a mix of indie and AAA titles and want Synology’s software polish.

 In my test, I moved 850GB of Steam games to a RAID 5 array on the DXP4800 Plus, then ran Cyberpunk 2077 from the network share over a 10GbE connection. Load times were within 5% of my internal NVMe drive, and in-game streaming of textures showed zero pop-in. The 1,250 MB/s media speed is not just marketing fluff; it shows up in real-world Steam downloads and game installations.
 UGREEN’s UGOS Pro interface took me about 20 minutes to learn, and after that, managing the Steam library share, snapshots, and Docker containers felt second nature. I also ran a Steam caching server in a Docker container, and the DXP4800 Plus had CPU headroom to spare.
 The 8GB DDR5 RAM is enough for Steam hosting plus a Plex server plus a few Docker apps. I bumped it to 16GB during testing, and the system handled 4K transcoding and a Steam library sync without breaking a sweat. Storage capacity scales to 144TB across four bays plus two M.2 NVMe slots, and that is overkill for most Steam libraries but great for media hoarders.
 iSCSI vs SMB for Steam games
 I tested both protocols side by side on the DXP4800 Plus, and iSCSI delivered noticeably lower latency for game launches. SMB is easier to set up (just create a share and map it), and modern SMB 3.0 multichannel support closes the gap on 2.5GbE or faster networks. For the best Steam gaming experience over network, I recommend iSCSI presented as a local block device.
 Setting up iSCSI on the DXP4800 Plus required creating a LUN in UGOS Pro, then connecting from Windows using the Microsoft iSCSI Initiator. Once mounted, Windows treats the iSCSI target as a local drive, and Steam sees no difference between it and a SATA SSD. Random read latency dropped by 1.5-2ms compared to SMB in my benchmarks.
 Real-world Steam load times
 Testing Cyberpunk 2077, Baldur’s Gate 3, and Counter-Strike 2 from the DXP4800 Plus over 10GbE gave me load times within 5-8% of internal NVMe. Counter-Strike 2, which is very sensitive to storage latency, was completely indistinguishable from a local SSD install. Baldur’s Gate 3 took 47 seconds over the NAS versus 44 seconds on internal storage.
 The only scenario where the DXP4800 Plus showed weakness was running multiple heavy game launches simultaneously. With two clients doing fresh Steam library scans, throughput dropped to around 800 MB/s, which is still fast. For a single gamer, this is the sweet spot of performance and value.

 I configured link aggregation to combine both 10GbE ports, and the result was a Steam library that loaded games faster than a SATA SSD install. Baldur’s Gate 3, which normally takes 44 seconds to launch from my internal NVMe, loaded in 41 seconds from the DXP4800 GT with a 144TB RAID 5 array. That is a 7% improvement, and it speaks to how fast NVMe cache plus 10GbE networking can be.
 The AMD Ryzen R2514 is a 4-core, 8-thread CPU that clocks up to 3.70GHz, and it chews through Steam updates, Docker containers, and Plex transcoding without breaking a sweat. I had a Steam caching server, Plex, Home Assistant, and a game server all running simultaneously, and CPU usage never crossed 60%.
 UGREEN’s build quality is excellent. The aluminum chassis feels premium, the SD card slot on the front is great for quickly offloading photos from a camera, and the local AI photo management is a nice bonus if you also use the NAS for family photos. The dual 10GbE ports are also future-proof, since 10GbE switches keep getting cheaper.
 Setting up dual 10GbE for maximum game throughput
 To get full dual 10GbE performance, you need a managed switch that supports LACP (Link Aggregation Control Protocol) or you can use SMB 3.0 multichannel if both your NAS and PC have 10GbE NICs. I tested both, and SMB multichannel was easier to configure on Windows 11.
 Once configured, large game installations that used to saturate gigabit ethernet (taking 30 minutes for a 100GB game) completed in 4 minutes over the dual 10GbE setup. That alone makes the DXP4800 GT worth it for gamers who regularly install large AAA titles.
 Limitations to be aware of
 The biggest limitation is the 8GB DDR4 RAM, which is enough for most Steam library use cases but limits how many Docker containers you can run. I bumped mine to 32GB, and the system recognized all of it without issues. The other limitation is the smaller community compared to Synology, so finding troubleshooting tips for edge cases takes more effort.
 NAS beginners may find the initial UGOS Pro setup slightly overwhelming compared to Synology’s guided wizard. If you have never set up a NAS before, budget an extra hour for the learning curve. Power users will feel right at home.

 Why NVMe-only NAS is great for gaming
 Games with asset streaming (Cyberpunk 2077, Microsoft Flight Simulator, Star Citizen) need fast random read performance. Mechanical hard drives and even SATA SSDs struggle with the constant small file requests that game engines make. NVMe SSDs deliver over 500,000 IOPS for random 4K reads, and that translates to smoother in-game streaming and faster texture loads.
 The AS5402T lets you build an all-NVMe pool without needing a separate SSD cache. With four M.2 slots, you can balance capacity and performance. I used 2TB drives in RAID 5 for 6TB usable, but you could also run RAID 10 for maximum performance with 4TB usable.
 Where the AS5402T falls short
 Software is the main weak point. ADM has improved a lot, but it is still not as refined as DSM. Firmware updates occasionally introduce bugs, and the Asustor community is smaller than Synology’s. If you are a hands-on user who likes to tinker, you will be fine. If you want a set-and-forget experience, Synology is still the safer bet.
 Storage capacity is also limited compared to 4-bay HDD NAS units. With 2TB NVMe drives, you max out at 8TB raw (6TB in RAID 5). For most Steam libraries that is plenty, but media hoarders will need bigger spinning rust.

 NVMe cache configuration for gaming

 Write cache is less useful for gaming workloads unless you are also recording gameplay or installing new games frequently. The DS925+ supports up to two NVMe SSDs for cache, and Synology’s own branded drives are expensive but well-supported. Third-party drives now work after Synology’s policy reversal.

 Buying Guide: How to Choose the Best NAS for Steam Gaming?
 Choosing the right NAS for hosting your Steam library comes down to four key factors: network speed, drive configuration, CPU power, and protocol support. Let me walk through each one so you can match the right NAS to your gaming setup.
 Network speed: gigabit is the bare minimum
 Gigabit ethernet caps out at around 115 MB/s in real-world throughput, which is fine for indie games and older titles. For modern AAA games with constant asset streaming, you really want 2.5GbE at a minimum. If you have the budget and infrastructure, 10GbE is the sweet spot for Steam library hosting.
 I tested all 8 NAS units over 2.5GbE and 10GbE, and the difference was night and day for modern games. Cyberpunk 2077 loaded in 38 seconds over 10GbE versus 52 seconds over gigabit. Counter-Strike 2 felt identical to internal storage over 10GbE, but showed minor stutters over gigabit during intense firefights.
 For most gamers, a 2.5GbE NAS like the Synology DS225+ or Asustor AS5402T is the sweet spot. 2.5GbE switches are now under $50, and the Cat 5e cables you already have will work. If you are building a new network from scratch, go straight to 10GbE with the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus or DXP4800 GT.
 Drive configuration: HDDs, SSDs, or both
 For a pure Steam library NAS, NVMe SSDs deliver the best gaming experience by a wide margin. The random read performance of NVMe is 50-100x faster than spinning rust, and that matters for games that constantly stream assets. The Asustor AS5402T with four NVMe drives is the budget NVMe champion.
 If you have a massive library (5TB+), HDDs are more cost-effective. A 4-bay NAS with 18TB drives gives you 54TB of usable space in RAID 5, which is enough for any Steam library plus a media collection. Pair HDDs with NVMe cache for the best of both worlds.
 Steam library performance on a pure HDD NAS is playable but not ideal. Games with loading screens work fine, but open-world games will show texture pop-in. If you go with HDDs, budget for NVMe cache to accelerate hot game data.
 Protocol choice: SMB vs iSCSI for Steam
 SMB is the easiest protocol to set up and works well for most gaming scenarios. Modern SMB 3.0 with multichannel support can saturate 2.5GbE or even 10GbE. For casual gamers, SMB is the right choice.
 iSCSI delivers lower latency than SMB, especially for random read workloads. The setup is more complex (you need to use the Microsoft iSCSI Initiator on Windows), but the performance benefit is worth it for serious gamers. Random read latency dropped by 1.5-2ms on the DXP4800 Plus when I switched from SMB to iSCSI.
 For Steam specifically, either protocol works. The difference shows up most in game launch times and texture streaming. If you want every last millisecond of performance, go with iSCSI. If you want simplicity, SMB is fine.
 CPU and RAM: matching horsepower to workload
 For pure Steam library hosting, a quad-core CPU and 4GB of RAM is enough. The Intel N5105 found in the Asustor AS5402T and AS6706T handles Steam hosting plus light Docker use without breaking a sweat. If you also want to run Plex, Home Assistant, or game servers, step up to 8GB or more.
 The Intel Core i3-1315U in the UGREEN DXP4800 Pro and the AMD Ryzen R2514 in the DXP4800 GT are overkill for Steam hosting alone, but they give you headroom for everything else. If your NAS is also your home server, these CPUs are worth the premium.
 RAM matters more than CPU for gaming workloads. Steam hosting is not CPU intensive, but more RAM lets you run more concurrent services. 4GB is the minimum, 8GB is the sweet spot, and 16GB+ is for power users running VMs.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Can you put a Steam library on a NAS?
 Yes, you can put your Steam library on a NAS. Steam treats a network share as a standard library folder, so you can install and launch games directly from the NAS just like a local drive. For the best experience, use a NAS with 2.5GbE or 10GbE networking and either SSD storage or HDD with NVMe cache.
 Can I run Steam games off a NAS?
 Yes, you can run Steam games directly from a NAS over the network. Modern games with constant asset streaming (Cyberpunk 2077, Star Citizen, Microsoft Flight Simulator) need at least 2.5GbE networking and ideally SSD storage on the NAS. Older games with loading screens work fine even on gigabit ethernet with HDD storage.
 What is the best NAS for storing games?
 The best NAS for storing games is the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus thanks to its 10GbE port, Intel 8505 CPU, and dual M.2 NVMe slots. It delivers gaming performance within 5% of internal NVMe storage over a 10GbE network. For budget buyers, the Asustor AS5402T with four NVMe slots is a great alternative.
 Is NAS worth it for gaming?
 NAS is worth it for gaming if you have a large Steam library (1TB+) that you want to access from multiple PCs, or if you want to centralize your game storage and media in one device. For a single gaming PC with a small library, internal SSD storage is still simpler and faster. NAS gaming makes the most sense for households with multiple gaming setups.
 How fast does NAS need to be for gaming?
 For gaming on a NAS, you need at least gigabit ethernet for older games, 2.5GbE for modern AAA titles, and 10GbE for the best possible experience. The NAS itself should have SSD storage (NVMe preferred) or HDD with NVMe cache. Random read performance matters more than sequential throughput for game loading.
 Final Verdict: Which NAS Should You Buy for Steam Gaming?
 After three months of testing, the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus is the best NAS for gamers hosting Steam libraries for most people. The 10GbE port, Intel CPU, and dual M.2 NVMe slots deliver gaming performance within 5% of internal NVMe, and the price is reasonable for what you get.
 Budget buyers should grab the Asustor AS5402T for its four NVMe slots and 2.5GbE networking. Synology loyalists will love the DS225+ or DS925+ for their software polish, even if the hardware is not class-leading. Power users with massive libraries should look at the Asustor Lockerstor 6 Gen2 AS6706T for its 6-bay capacity plus 4 NVMe slots.
 Whatever you choose, make sure your network is at least 2.5GbE, and your storage is SSD-based or backed by NVMe cache. That combination is what separates a playable NAS gaming experience from a frustrating one. Happy gaming in 2026.

The best NAS for gamers should do more than store old files. A good system can back up save data, archive large game libraries, host media, share files between gaming PCs, and serve fast local storage. For serious use, prioritize 2.5GbE or 10GbE networking, multiple drive bays, NVMe support, and reliable software.

 1. UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus
 Best For: Gamers who want fast networking and strong hardware
 The UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus is a compelling gaming NAS because it combines four SATA bays with two M.2 slots and both 10GbE and 2.5GbE Ethernet. That network configuration gives a modern gaming PC far more transfer headroom than a standard Gigabit NAS when moving very large game archives or media files.
 Its Intel Pentium Gold 8505 processor uses five cores and six threads, while the system includes 8GB of DDR5 memory that can be expanded significantly. That hardware gives the NAS enough flexibility for file serving, backups, Docker workloads, media management, and other tasks that may run alongside normal game-library storage.
 For gamers, the 10GbE connection is the standout feature. A fast desktop fitted with a compatible 10GbE adapter can move data far faster than through Gigabit Ethernet, assuming the drives, RAID configuration, switch, and client storage can keep up. This matters most when transferring hundreds of gigabytes rather than launching individual games.
 The two M.2 slots also provide useful options for NVMe storage or acceleration, depending on how the system is configured. That can help a mixed workload involving small files, applications, containers, and frequently accessed data. It does not automatically make hard drives behave like SSDs, so expectations should remain realistic.
 Best NAS for Gamers at a Glance 
 Key Features
 Four SATA drive bays
 Two M.2 SSD slots
 Intel Pentium Gold 8505 processor
 8GB DDR5 memory
 Memory expansion support
 One 10GbE LAN port
 One 2.5GbE LAN port
 RAID 0, 1, 5, 6, and 10 support
 HDMI output
 USB-C and USB-A connectivity
 What Makes It Different
 The DXP4800 Plus gives gamers 10GbE without requiring an expansion card. That makes it easier to build a high-speed storage path between a gaming desktop and NAS from the start, while the four HDD bays still provide the capacity advantage that makes network storage useful for large libraries, recordings, and backups.
 Pros
 Native 10GbE networking
 Additional 2.5GbE port
 Four SATA bays
 Two M.2 slots
 Expandable DDR5 memory
 Strong hardware for a home NAS
 Cons
 Fast networking requires matching client hardware
 10GbE switches and adapters add cost
 Newer software ecosystem than long-established rivals
 Use Case: Large game archives, PC backups, gameplay recordings, media libraries, Docker workloads, and fast file transfers between multiple computers.
 Who It’s For: Gamers who want strong hardware and 10GbE without immediately adding a separate network expansion card.
 2. QNAP TS-464
 Best For: Gamers who want expansion flexibility
 The QNAP TS-464 is a four-bay NAS with two 2.5GbE network ports, two M.2 NVMe slots, and a PCIe expansion slot. That combination is useful for gamers who want solid performance now but may later upgrade the system with faster networking or additional storage hardware as the rest of the home network evolves.
 QNAP uses an Intel Celeron N5095 processor with integrated graphics, and the TS-464 supports hardware-accelerated video transcoding. This makes it more versatile than a pure file server because the same NAS can store game captures, run a media library, and convert compatible video for playback on different devices.
 The two 2.5GbE ports are useful even without a 10GbE upgrade. A single 2.5GbE connection already offers much more theoretical bandwidth than Gigabit Ethernet, while QNAP also supports link aggregation for suitable workloads. Gamers should remember that one client connection does not automatically become a single 5Gbps stream.
 The PCIe slot is what gives the TS-464 long-term appeal. QNAP supports optional faster network adapters, including 10GbE solutions, which means the NAS can grow with a faster switch and desktop adapter later. This avoids replacing the entire enclosure simply because the home network moves beyond 2.5GbE.
 Key Features
 Four SATA drive bays
 Two M.2 2280 NVMe slots
 Dual 2.5GbE LAN
 PCIe expansion slot
 Optional 10GbE expansion
 Intel Celeron N5095 processor
 Hardware video transcoding

 USB 3.2 Gen 2 ports
 QTS or supported QuTS hero configuration
 What Makes It Different
 The TS-464 is unusually flexible for a compact four-bay NAS. It can begin as a dual-2.5GbE storage server and later gain faster networking through PCIe. That makes it attractive to gamers who expect their setup to change over several years and do not want networking capability permanently fixed at purchase.
 Pros
 Dual 2.5GbE ports
 PCIe expansion
 Two NVMe slots
 Hardware transcoding
 HDMI output
 Mature feature-rich NAS software
 Cons

 Advanced software has a learning curve
 M.2 interface is not designed for maximum desktop NVMe speeds
 Use Case: Game backups, Plex-style media libraries, PC backups, virtualization, game recording archives, and expandable home networking.
 Who It’s For: Gamers who want a NAS that can be upgraded rather than replaced as storage and networking requirements increase.
 3. Synology DS925+
 Best For: Gamers who prioritize simple backups and software
 Synology DS925+ is a four-bay NAS focused heavily on data management, backup, synchronization, and long-term storage. It uses an AMD Ryzen V1500B processor with four cores and eight threads, includes 4GB of ECC DDR4 memory, and supports expansion to 32GB for heavier services and multitasking.
 Networking improves significantly over older Gigabit Synology systems because the DS925+ includes two 2.5GbE Ethernet ports. Synology also provides two M.2 NVMe slots that can be used for compatible SSD cache or storage-pool configurations, giving users more options for frequently accessed data.
 The main attraction is DiskStation Manager rather than raw specification dominance. DSM provides mature backup, file synchronization, snapshots, remote access, user management, and media applications in a relatively consistent interface. For a gamer storing valuable recordings and personal files, software reliability can matter as much as speed.
 Its biggest limitation for performance-focused users is the lack of native 10GbE. Dual 2.5GbE is enough for many households and comfortably exceeds Gigabit networking, but gamers trying to approach local NVMe-style transfer speeds across the network will find faster 10GbE-equipped alternatives more appropriate.
 Key Features

 What Makes It Different
 The DS925+ is less about chasing maximum bandwidth and more about providing a polished storage environment. Gamers who primarily need dependable backups, shared files, save archives, screenshots, recordings, and media libraries may value DSM’s organization and protection tools more than an unused 10GbE connection.

 Who It’s For: Gamers who prioritize easy storage management and dependable backup workflows over maximum network throughput.
 4. ASUSTOR Lockerstor 4 Gen2+
 Best For: Gamers who want multiple NVMe drives
 The ASUSTOR Lockerstor 4 Gen2+ combines four conventional SATA bays with four M.2 NVMe slots, giving it unusually broad solid-state storage flexibility for a four-bay NAS. It uses an Intel Celeron N5105 processor and ships with 4GB of DDR4 memory, with expansion support up to 16GB.
 The updated Gen2+ model includes two 5GbE Ethernet ports, giving it more native bandwidth than typical dual-2.5GbE consumer NAS systems. This is useful for gaming households with several fast clients or a workstation that frequently moves large recording files, backups, mods, installers, and media across the network.
 Four M.2 slots create several configuration possibilities depending on the workload. Gamers can use NVMe storage for faster frequently accessed data while preserving larger HDD arrays for bulk storage. The exact benefit depends on configuration and workload, because sequential game archives behave differently from databases and many small files.
 ASUSTOR also provides HDMI output and hardware suitable for media-related use. This gives the NAS a role beyond storage when paired with the correct applications. For gamers, however, the main reason to choose it remains the combination of four SATA bays, multiple NVMe slots, and faster-than-Gigabit networking.
 Key Features
 Four SATA drive bays
 Four M.2 NVMe slots
 Intel Celeron N5105 processor
 4GB DDR4 memory
 Up to 16GB memory support
 Dual 5GbE Ethernet
 USB 3.2 Gen 2
 HDMI output
 RAID support

 What Makes It Different
 Four M.2 slots make the Lockerstor 4 Gen2+ much more flexible than systems offering only one or two NVMe positions. Gamers building mixed HDD and SSD storage can keep large capacity drives for archives while dedicating faster solid-state space to workloads that benefit more from lower latency and higher random performance.
 Pros

 Dual 5GbE networking
 Four SATA bays
 Expandable memory
 Good media capabilities
 Strong mixed-storage flexibility

 Use Case: Game archives, SSD-backed network shares, content creation, media streaming, backups, and enthusiast home servers.
 Who It’s For: Gamers who specifically want more NVMe flexibility than most four-bay consumer NAS systems provide.
 5. TerraMaster F4-424 Max
 Best For: High-performance gaming storage and home labs
 The TerraMaster F4-424 Max is the most performance-oriented system in this group. It uses an Intel Core i5-1235U with ten cores and twelve threads, includes 8GB of DDR5 memory, and provides two native 10GbE ports. That hardware gives it considerably more compute and network headroom than a typical entry-level NAS.
 Dual 10GbE is especially useful in a gaming and creator household where more than one powerful system needs fast storage access. The ports can also support aggregated bandwidth in suitable network configurations, although one normal client transfer will still be limited by its own network link and the storage array’s performance.
 Two M.2 NVMe slots provide SSD caching options alongside the four SATA bays. Combined with the Core i5 processor, this makes the system suitable for more than simple file sharing. Virtual machines, databases, containers, media processing, and other home-lab tasks can coexist with a large gaming archive more comfortably.
 The trade-off is cost and complexity. Gamers who only want to back up one PC do not need this level of processing power or network bandwidth. The F4-424 Max makes the most sense when the NAS is becoming an important central server for gaming storage, content creation, media, virtualization, and household data.
 Key Features
 Four SATA drive bays
 Intel Core i5-1235U
 Ten cores and twelve threads
 8GB DDR5 memory
 Dual 10GbE Ethernet
 Two M.2 NVMe slots
 Integrated Intel graphics
 Hardware encryption support
 High-speed home-server capability
 TerraMaster TOS ecosystem
 What Makes It Different
 The Core i5 processor and dual 10GbE networking move the F4-424 Max closer to a compact server than a basic home NAS. Gamers who also stream, edit video, run virtual machines, maintain home-lab services, or transfer very large files can use the extra resources instead of operating several separate computers.
 Pros
 Dual 10GbE networking
 Powerful Core i5 CPU
 DDR5 memory
 Two NVMe slots
 Excellent multi-service potential
 Strong fit for advanced home labs
 Cons
 Overkill for basic backup
 Fast infrastructure increases total cost
 More powerful hardware can consume more energy than entry-level NAS units
 Use Case: High-speed storage, large game archives, multiple gaming PCs, virtual machines, Docker, media servers, and creator workloads.
 Who It’s For: Enthusiasts who want one powerful NAS to handle gaming storage and several advanced home-server roles.
 How to Choose the Best NAS for Gamers
 Start With Network Speed
 A NAS can contain very fast drives while still feeling slow if the connection is limited to Gigabit Ethernet. For large game files, 2.5GbE is a useful baseline, while 5GbE or 10GbE becomes more attractive for users moving hundreds of gigabytes regularly. The gaming PC, switch, and NAS all need compatible networking.
 Understand Game Storage Limitations
 A NAS is excellent for storing installers, backups, recordings, ROM libraries, and archived games, but not every modern PC game is designed to run directly from a network share. Anti-cheat systems, launchers, file locking, latency, and installation requirements can make local SSD storage the safer choice for active AAA libraries.
 Use the NAS as a Fast Archive
 One practical approach is to keep currently played games on the local NVMe SSD and move inactive libraries or installation data to the NAS. When storage becomes tight, files can be transferred back instead of downloading everything again. Faster 2.5GbE or 10GbE networking makes this workflow much more convenient.
 Choose Enough Drive Bays
 Two-bay NAS systems are compact, but four bays provide greater flexibility for capacity and RAID layouts. Gamers accumulating recordings, media, backups, and project files can outgrow two drives surprisingly quickly. A four-bay enclosure provides more room to balance usable capacity, redundancy, and future expansion.
 Do Not Treat RAID as Backup
 RAID can protect availability when a drive fails, but it does not protect against accidental deletion, malware, theft, fire, or catastrophic hardware failure. Important game saves, personal files, and creator projects should also exist on another device or cloud service rather than depending entirely on one NAS array.
 NVMe Slots Can Be Useful
 M.2 slots can support cache or dedicated SSD storage depending on the NAS platform. They are most useful when workloads involve many small files, applications, databases, or fast network storage. For sequential archives stored on hard drives, adding NVMe does not automatically transform every transfer into desktop-SSD performance.
 Consider Media Transcoding
 Gamers often use the same NAS for movies, gameplay recordings, and streaming. Intel processors with integrated graphics can be useful when media applications support hardware transcoding. If every device can direct-play the stored video format, however, transcoding performance becomes less important than storage capacity and network speed.
 Think About Noise
 A NAS containing several mechanical hard drives can produce audible seek noise and vibration. If the enclosure must sit beside the gaming desk, drive selection and fan behavior matter. Placing the NAS elsewhere on the wired network can keep storage noise away from the gaming position without sacrificing access speed.
 NAS vs External SSD for Game Storage
 An external SSD is simpler when only one gaming PC needs extra capacity. It connects directly, offers low latency, and requires no network configuration. For active games, an external SSD can therefore be easier than a NAS, assuming the game launcher and interface support the chosen external storage device correctly.
 A NAS becomes more useful when several devices need the same data or when backup, redundancy, remote access, media serving, and centralized storage matter. It costs more initially but can consolidate many roles. The best setup often combines a fast local gaming SSD with a larger NAS for shared storage and protection.
 FAQ
 Can You Play PC Games Directly From a NAS?
 Sometimes, but it is not the ideal approach for every game. Network file behavior, launchers, anti-cheat software, and latency can create problems even when transfer speed is high. A safer workflow is keeping active games on local SSD storage and using the NAS for archives, backups, installers, and less demanding content.
 Is 2.5GbE Enough for a Gaming NAS?
 Yes, for many users. A 2.5GbE link offers far more bandwidth than standard Gigabit Ethernet and can make large backups and transfers significantly faster. Users with fast SSD arrays, multiple clients, or very large creator workloads may benefit from 5GbE or 10GbE, but those speeds require matching network hardware.
 Is 10GbE Worth It for Gamers?
 It is worth considering when you frequently move hundreds of gigabytes between the NAS and a fast PC or use the same system for video production and other large files. It will not reduce in-game ping or improve GPU performance. The advantage is faster local data transfer, not faster internet gaming.
 How Many NAS Bays Do Gamers Need?
 Four bays offer a good balance for serious home storage because they provide more RAID and capacity options than two-bay systems while remaining compact. A two-bay model can still work for smaller libraries, while larger systems become useful when multiple PCs, media libraries, and creator projects share the same storage.
 Should a Gaming NAS Use HDDs or SSDs?
 Hard drives remain useful for large, cost-efficient archives, while SSDs offer lower latency, silence, and higher performance. Many gaming NAS setups benefit from combining both: HDDs for bulk storage and NVMe or SATA SSDs for selected high-speed workloads. The correct mix depends on capacity and network speed.
 Does a NAS Improve Gaming Performance?
 A NAS does not increase FPS or lower internet latency. Its benefit is storage management: centralized backups, faster access to archives, media serving, and sharing files between systems. The most noticeable gaming advantage is convenience when large local files can be restored quickly instead of downloaded again.
 Conclusion
 The best NAS for gamers depends on whether you value raw transfer speed, storage software, or expansion. UGREEN DXP4800 Plus offers native 10GbE, QNAP TS-464 favors upgrades, Synology DS925+ excels at management, ASUSTOR adds four NVMe slots, and TerraMaster F4-424 Max targets demanding high-speed home servers.

results.title: Best Prosumer NAS: 10GbE and NVMe (2026)
results.text:
Best Prosumer NAS: 10GbE and NVMe (2026) 
 As an Amazon Associate we earn from qualifying purchases. Prices and availability come from Amazon.com as of the last update and may change.
 Quick answer
 The best prosumer NAS combines 10GbE networking, NVMe storage pools or cache and ECC memory, which is exactly what the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus (10GbE built in) and Synology DS923+ (ECC plus optional 10GbE) deliver. The QNAP TS-464 is the choice if you want the most ports, dual 2.5GbE, HDMI and M.2 in one box. Pick 10GbE when you edit large files off the NAS, and remember 2.5GbE is plenty for backups and streaming.
 As of November 3, 2026

 What makes a NAS prosumer-grade
 Prosumer sits between a basic home box and full business kit. The buyer wants performance and features that enthusiasts and power users appreciate: fast 10GbE networking, NVMe storage for speed, ECC memory for integrity, and the headroom to run virtual machines, containers and demanding apps. It is about capability and flexibility rather than the simplest possible setup.
 10GbE is the headline feature. It transforms the experience if you edit large photo or video files directly off the NAS, where gigabit and even 2.5GbE would bottleneck you. The DXP4800 Plus builds 10GbE in, the DS923+ accepts an optional 10GbE card, and you pair either with a matching switch and computer. That said, be honest about your needs: 2.5GbE is genuinely plenty for backups, file sharing and media streaming, so 10GbE is for off-NAS editing rather than everyday tasks.
 NVMe and ECC round out the package. NVMe drives can serve as a fast cache or, on supporting platforms, a separate fast storage pool for active work. ECC memory corrects rare errors for data integrity, which power users running important data appreciate. Add generous expandable memory, like the DXP4800 Plus's DDR5 to 32GB or the DS923+'s ECC DDR4 to 32GB, and you have a box that keeps up with heavier workloads.
 Best prosumer NAS by priority
 Use case Best choice Why 
 10GbE built in UGREEN DXP4800 Plus Pentium Gold 8505, 10GbE plus 2.5GbE, DDR5 to 32GB and dual NVMe out of the box. 
 ECC integrity plus 10GbE option Synology DS923+ AMD Ryzen, ECC DDR4 to 32GB, dual NVMe and an optional 10GbE card with the best software. 
 Most ports and connectivity QNAP TS-464 Dual 2.5GbE, HDMI out and M.2 slots for a flexible, hardware-rich build. 
 NVMe pools for active work DXP4800 Plus or DS923+ Dual NVMe slots can cache or, where supported, run a fast pool for current projects. 
 How much to budget
 Plan the appliance, the spinning drives and the NVMe drives as one cost. The enclosure price is just the start, and a prosumer build adds NVMe for cache or a fast pool plus, often, a memory upgrade. The drives commonly cost as much as the box or more once you size them properly.
 For the main storage pool use NAS-rated CMR drives such as WD Red Plus or Red Pro, Seagate IronWolf or IronWolf Pro, and Toshiba N300, with Seagate Exos for the best price per terabyte at high capacity. Avoid SMR drives in RAID. Then budget separately for the NVMe drives and, if you are going 10GbE, a compatible switch and cabling, because the network is only as fast as its slowest link.
 Spend in line with how you will actually use the box. If you edit off the NAS, prioritise 10GbE and NVMe. If you mainly back up and stream, save the money: a 2.5GbE prosumer box with a sensible RAID pool will feel fast and leave budget for more capacity.

 Frequently asked questions
 Do I actually need 10GbE?
 Only if you edit large photo or video files directly off the NAS, where it removes the network bottleneck. For backups, file sharing and streaming, 2.5GbE is genuinely plenty. The DXP4800 Plus builds 10GbE in and the DS923+ takes a card, so you can choose based on your workflow.
 What is the point of NVMe slots on a prosumer NAS?
 NVMe drives can act as a fast read or write cache to speed up busy workloads, or on supporting platforms run as a separate fast pool for active projects. They are most useful for editing, databases and many concurrent users rather than basic file storage and backups.
 Why does ECC memory appear on prosumer models?
 ECC corrects rare memory errors that could otherwise corrupt data, which power users handling important files value. The DS923+ and DS925+ include ECC, and the DXP4800 Plus uses ECC-grade DDR5. It is one of the features that separates prosumer boxes from basic home units.
 Can a prosumer NAS run virtual machines and containers?
 Yes, the Intel and Ryzen prosumer models with expandable memory handle containers and light virtual machines well, which is part of their appeal. Adding memory, up to 64GB on the DXP4800 Plus and 32GB on the DS923+, gives the headroom to run several services alongside your storage.
 Is UGREEN or Synology the better prosumer choice?
 It depends on what you weigh most. UGREEN offers the best hardware value, including built-in 10GbE on the DXP4800 Plus. Synology offers the best software with DSM, SHR and its app ecosystem, plus ECC and a 10GbE option on the DS923+. QNAP wins on sheer ports and connectivity.

Best NAS for Home in 2026 — Backup, Photos and Plex | Loiter Point 
 Best NAS for Home in 2026
 Updated July 2026 · Loiter Point Storage Desk
 The Short Version
 Best overall / best for Plex: the UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus — a 4-bay box with a 5-core Pentium Gold, 8GB DDR5, two M.2 NVMe slots and a 10GbE port, which is genuinely rare at this money.
 Best software: the Synology DS925+ . DSM is still the most polished NAS operating system on the market. Caveat: no HDMI, and the Ryzen V1500B has no iGPU, so no hardware transcoding.
 Best value: the UGREEN NASync DXP2800 — N100, 8GB DDR5, 2.5GbE, dual M.2, aluminium chassis, usually under $320.
 Most horsepower per dollar: the TerraMaster F4-424 Pro (8-core i3-N305, 32GB DDR5) — if you can live with the least mature software of the three ecosystems.
 Grab your pick: 
 UGREEN DXP4800 Plus — MSRP $699.99, often ~$630 ·
 Synology DS925+ — ~$589.99 ·
 UGREEN DXP2800 — ~$296.99–$314 ·
 Synology DS224+ ·
 TerraMaster F4-424 Pro — ~$699.99 .
 All prices are street price at time of writing; NAS pricing swings hard with coupons and promos.
 A home NAS solves three problems at once: it gives every machine in the house a backup target, it gets your photo library off a cloud subscription and onto hardware you own, and it feeds Plex or Jellyfin without a laptop being left awake. The hard part of buying one in 2026 isn't finding capable hardware — it's that the four-figure decision is really about software, networking, and platform policy, none of which appear on the spec sheet in a useful way.
 This roundup picks five boxes across roughly $300 to $700, all sold diskless. Read the budget section at the bottom before you decide how much box you can afford, because drives usually cost as much as the NAS itself.
 How We Evaluate Home NAS Boxes
 Loiter Point does not run a lab, and we are not going to pretend otherwise. We do not own these units, we have not benchmarked them, and any number in this article that describes real-world behaviour is attributed to somebody who did the work.
 What we actually do: we synthesise published independent measurements and reviews, manufacturer specifications, and verified owner reports from support forums and retail feedback, then cross-check them against each other. Where those sources disagree — and on NAS transfer speeds they frequently do, because results depend heavily on the switch, the client NIC, and the drives fitted — we say so rather than picking the flattering number. Interface ceilings (1GbE, 2.5GbE, 10GbE) are quoted as theoretical maximums, not results. Spec rows marked "est. real-world" or "reported" are exactly that: estimates and third-party reports, never our measurements.
 We weight four things: the maturity of the software platform, because you live in it daily; networking headroom, because it is the most common bottleneck; transcoding capability, because it decides whether Plex works for remote users; and total cost including drives. We also weight vendor policy history, which is why the Synology section below is longer than the rest.
 The Five Picks
 #1 Best Overall · Best for Plex / Jellyfin 
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus
 MSRP $699.99 · frequently around $630, seen near $657 (street price at time of writing) 
 Bays
 4 × 3.5" SATA
 CPU
 Intel Pentium Gold 8505, 5-core, with iGPU
 RAM
 8GB DDR5, expandable
 Networking (rated)
 1 × 10GbE + 1 × 2.5GbE
 10GbE ceiling theoretical 
 ~1.1 GB/s, chain permitting
 Spinning-disk array throughput est. real-world 
 Typically saturates 2.5GbE, not 10GbE
 M.2 NVMe
 2 slots
 Extras
 128GB internal SSD, 4K HDMI out
 Pros
 10GbE at this price is close to unheard of
 Pentium Gold 8505 has an iGPU — hardware transcoding is on the table
 Two NVMe slots plus a built-in 128GB SSD for the OS and apps
 HDMI out means it can double as a local media player
 Cons
 UGOS Pro is a young OS; app ecosystem and long-term update record are thinner than DSM's
 10GbE only pays for itself if your switch and client can match it
 8GB is fine, but 4-bay users doing containers will want more
 This is the box we would point most people at. The hardware sheet reads like something a tier above the price: five cores with integrated graphics, DDR5, dual M.2, and a 10GbE port that competitors reserve for $900-plus models. For a household running Plex or Jellyfin with a couple of remote streams, the iGPU matters more than raw clock speed, and this has one.
 The honest counterweight is software. UGREEN's UGOS Pro is newer and less mature than Synology DSM — fewer first-party apps, a shorter track record on security updates, and a smaller community when something breaks at 11pm. If you are comfortable with Docker and don't need hand-holding, that trade is worth taking for the hardware. If you want the appliance to be boring, look at #2.
 Check price on Amazon 
 #2 Best Software · Best for Set-and-Forget 
 Synology DS925+
 Street around $589.99 · 90-day average ~$639.67 · hit $549.99 with a $90 coupon in Oct 2025 (street price at time of writing) 
 Bays

 Not available (no iGPU); direct play / direct stream fine
 M.2 NVMe

 None — no HDMI
 Pros
 DSM is the most polished, best-documented NAS OS you can buy
 ECC memory, expandable to 32GB
 Expandable to nine bays — the longest runway here
 Synology Photos and Hyper Backup are genuinely good first-party apps
 Cons
 No iGPU: hardware video transcoding is simply not available
 No HDMI output
 4GB base RAM is stingy at this price
 Carries the 2025 drive-policy history — see the nerd box below
 Buy the DS925+ for DSM. Snapshot replication, Hyper Backup to a second target, Synology Photos with face and subject recognition, and an update cadence that has been dependable for a decade — that's the product, and the hardware is a delivery mechanism for it. ECC RAM and nine-bay expansion also make this the pick if you expect the library to keep growing.
 Be clear-eyed about the media limitation. The Ryzen V1500B has no integrated GPU, so Plex cannot hardware-transcode on this box. If every client in your house direct-plays your files — which is typical for smart TVs and Apple TV with well-encoded libraries — you will never notice. If you routinely stream to phones on cellular, or you have a mixed bag of formats, pick #1 or #5 instead.
 Check price on Amazon 
 #3 Best Value 
 UGREEN NASync DXP2800
 List $349.99 · seen at $296.99 on Amazon US, around $314 with promo (street price at time of writing)

 Pros
 8GB DDR5 and dual M.2 at under $320 is unusually generous
 N100 has an iGPU — light transcoding is realistic

 Cons
 Two bays means limited redundancy options and a hard capacity ceiling
 Same UGOS Pro maturity caveat as the DXP4800 Plus
 N100 will run out of headroom with several simultaneous transcodes
 If you want the most competent hardware per dollar and don't need four bays, this is it. The spec list — N100, 8GB of DDR5, 2.5GbE, two NVMe slots, machined aluminium — reads like a $450 box. Android Central singled out the build quality as the best in the two-bay category, which matters more than it sounds for something that sits in a living room and runs continuously.
 The limitation is structural, not a flaw: two bays in a mirror gives you one drive of usable capacity and no room to grow without replacing both disks. If your photo and media library is already past a few terabytes, buy four bays now.
 Check price on Amazon 
 #4 Simplest Turnkey Backup + Photo Box 
 Synology DS224+
 Street pricing varies; check current listing (NAS prices move with coupons) 
 Bays
 2 × 3.5" SATA
 CPU
 Intel Celeron J4125, quad-core, with iGPU

 2GB DDR4, expandable
 Networking (rated)

 ~110 MB/s — the binding constraint on this box
 Hardware transcoding
 Available (J4125 iGPU)

 Pros
 Full DSM experience at the lowest entry point in this list
 J4125 does have an iGPU, unlike the pricier DS925+
 Genuinely turnkey: plug in, run the wizard, Synology Photos is working in twenty minutes
 Cons
 1GbE networking caps transfers around ~110 MB/s — no way around it
 2GB of RAM is tight; budget for an upgrade
 Older platform than everything else here
 We are recommending this one on honest terms: it is the oldest and slowest box in this roundup, and it is here because DSM on cheap hardware is still a better daily experience than a fast box with immature software. If your use case is "back up two laptops overnight and get my phone photos out of iCloud," 1GbE is adequate and you will never notice the ceiling.
 You will notice it the first time you dump a 200GB video project over the network. At roughly 110 MB/s theoretical — realistically less once protocol overhead is counted — that is a coffee break, not a moment. If large sequential transfers are part of your week, buy a 2.5GbE box instead, and pair it with a switch that can actually carry it; our home networking gear guide covers what to look for.
 Check price on Amazon 
 #5 Most Horsepower Per Dollar 
 TerraMaster F4-424 Pro
 Around $699.99 on Amazon · non-Pro F4-424 line starts around $499.99 · a 32GB config was seen at $559.99 in a deal (street price at time of writing) 
 Bays
 4 × 3.5" SATA
 CPU
 Intel Core i3-N305, 8-core / 8-thread, with iGPU
 RAM
 32GB DDR5
 Networking (rated)

 Aggregate 2.5GbE ceiling theoretical 
 ~280 MB/s per link; link aggregation needs a capable switch
 Media performance reported

 Software
 TerraMaster TNAS
 Pros
 8-core i3-N305 with 32GB of DDR5 is far more compute than anything else here
 Neowin called it the most powerful media-class 4-bay NAS on the market; XDA called it a powerful NAS at a reasonable price
 Enough headroom for multiple containers, VMs and transcodes at once
 Cons
 TNAS is the least mature of the three ecosystems here — firmware maturity is the real tradeoff
 No 10GbE despite the compute to use it
 Priced at the same level as the DXP4800 Plus, which has faster networking
 Pure compute, this wins and it isn't close. Eight cores and 32GB of DDR5 give you room to run Plex, Immich, a few Docker services and a light VM simultaneously without the box thinking about it. Reviewers have been consistent on the value of the hardware: Neowin's framing of it as the most powerful media-class 4-bay on the market matches XDA's read of it as a lot of NAS for the money.
 The reservation is the platform. TNAS has historically been the least polished of the three software stacks in this article, and TerraMaster has had a rougher security and firmware history than Synology. That is a real risk for a box holding your only copy of the family photos — it is manageable if you keep the NAS off the open internet, patch promptly, and maintain an off-box backup, which you should be doing regardless.
 Check price on Amazon 
 Nerd Box: The Synology Drive-Lock Saga
 In early 2025 Synology introduced a drive-compatibility policy that made third-party hard drives — Seagate IronWolf, WD Red Plus, the standard NAS drives everyone owns — effectively unusable in its 2025-generation models, including the DS925+, DS1825+ and DS425+. The unit would refuse to complete setup with an unverified drive. Not a warning banner: a hard stop.
 After significant backlash, Synology reversed course in DSM 7.3, released October 2025. Third-party HDDs and 2.5" SATA SSDs are now accepted on those models without warnings or restrictions. The caveat that still applies, and that buyers keep missing: the reversal does not extend to M.2 NVMe drives. Creating an M.2 storage pool still requires drives from Synology's official compatibility list, so if you were planning to drop a pair of cheap consumer NVMe sticks into the DS925+ for caching, check the list first.
 We are including this history because the fix does not make the episode irrelevant. Platform policy — what the vendor can decide about your hardware after you have bought it, via a firmware update — is part of what you are purchasing. Synology reversed this one under pressure, which is a reasonable sign. It is still worth knowing the policy existed. (Sources: Tom's Hardware, Synology Knowledge Center, NASCompares.)
 Nerd Box: Networking Is Usually the Real Bottleneck
 Interface ceilings, as theoretical maximums rather than measured results: 1GbE tops out around 110 MB/s , 2.5GbE around 280 MB/s , and 10GbE around 1.1 GB/s . You only see those numbers if every link in the chain keeps up — the switch, the client's NIC, the cabling, and critically the drives themselves.
 That last one is where 10GbE marketing gets ahead of reality. A four-drive array of spinning disks will typically saturate 2.5GbE comfortably but will not come close to filling a 10GbE pipe. Ten-gigabit mainly pays off when you add NVMe caching or run an all-SSD array. Buying a 10GbE NAS and plugging it into a 1GbE switch buys you nothing at all — check your switch and your client machine before you pay for the port. If your network is the weak link, start with our guides to Wi-Fi routers and mesh Wi-Fi systems , and remember that Wi-Fi 6E or 7 clients will still be slower to the NAS than a wired 2.5GbE link.
 All Five Compared
 Model Bays CPU RAM Networking M.2 Street price 
 UGREEN DXP4800 Plus 4 Pentium Gold 8505 (5-core, iGPU) 8GB DDR5, exp. 10GbE + 2.5GbE 2 MSRP $699.99; often ~$630 
 Synology DS925+ 4 (to 9) Ryzen V1500B (4-core, no iGPU) 4GB ECC, to 32GB 2 × 2.5GbE 2 ~$589.99 
 UGREEN DXP2800 2 Intel N100 (4-core, iGPU) 8GB DDR5 2.5GbE 2 ~$296.99–$314 
 Synology DS224+ 2 Celeron J4125 (4-core, iGPU) 2GB, exp. 2 × 1GbE — Check listing 
 TerraMaster F4-424 Pro 4 Core i3-N305 (8-core, iGPU) 32GB DDR5 2 × 2.5GbE Yes ~$699.99 
 All prices are street price at time of writing and move frequently with coupons and promotional pricing. Verify before buying.
 What Else You Need to Budget For
 Drives. Every box in this article ships diskless. This is the single most common budgeting mistake — filling four bays with NAS-rated drives often costs as much as the NAS itself, sometimes more, and it means the real entry price of a 4-bay build is well north of $1,000. Decide your capacity target first, then work backwards to the chassis you can afford. Buy NAS-rated drives; desktop drives in a 24/7 vibrating four-bay array are a false economy.
 A UPS. Strongly recommended, not optional in our view. A NAS is a computer that is always on, always holding dirty write caches, and running a filesystem that does not enjoy sudden power loss. Every OS here supports graceful shutdown triggered by a USB-connected UPS. A basic line-interactive unit is cheap insurance against a rebuild — see our UPS and battery backup picks for sizing.
 An actual backup. RAID is not a backup. RAID protects against a drive failing; it does nothing about ransomware, a bad delete, a failed controller, a fire, or a theft. Follow 3-2-1: three copies of the data, on two different media types, with one copy off-site. In practice that means the NAS plus a cloud target or a rotating portable SSD you keep somewhere else. Synology's Hyper Backup and standard tools like restic or rclone all handle this.
 Bottom Line
 For most households the UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus is the right buy: four bays, an iGPU that makes Plex behave, dual M.2, and 10GbE you can grow into, at a price where competitors give you 2.5GbE and a slower chip. The cost is a younger software platform.
 If you would rather the appliance be boring and dependable, buy the Synology DS925+ and accept that hardware transcoding is off the table — just go in knowing the 2025 drive-policy history and the M.2 compatibility-list caveat that survived the reversal. On a tighter budget, the UGREEN DXP2800 is the value play and the Synology DS224+ is the simplest possible on-ramp if you can live with 1GbE. And if you want maximum compute and are comfortable managing a less mature platform yourself, the TerraMaster F4-424 Pro gives you eight cores and 32GB for the money.
 Whichever you pick: budget for the drives, put it behind a UPS, and set up an off-box backup on day one. The hardware choice matters far less than doing those three things.

As high-resolution content, real-time collaboration, and data-intensive gaming continue to evolve, home networks must keep pace. For many media professionals and gaming enthusiasts, traditional Gigabit Ethernet is increasingly insufficient for the scale and velocity of modern workflows. This is where 10-Gigabit Ethernet (10GbE) NAS solutions emerge as the backbone of a future-ready digital environment. This article provides a clear, technically grounded perspective on 10GbE NAS adoption, while helping buyers of different technical backgrounds understand how to build and optimize a next-generation storage and gaming infrastructure.

Why 10GbE NAS Matters in 2025 and Beyond

The acceleration of 4K/8K video production, high-asset gaming libraries, and AI-supported content processing has created sustained demand for fast, centralized, and secure storage. A 10GbE NAS provides several distinct advantages:

1. True High-Bandwidth Performance

10GbE supports transfer speeds of up to 1,200 MB/s—roughly 10 times that of traditional Gigabit Ethernet—making it suitable for multi-stream editing, large game library hosting, and rapid data ingestion for AI-enhanced tools.

2. Centralized Workflow Efficiency

Whether you are rendering high-resolution footage or running texture-heavy game mods across multiple devices, a NAS consolidates assets into one scalable hub. This reduces redundancy and simplifies version control.

3. Long-Term Scalability

A 10GbE network provides ample headroom for future growth, especially as home labs and prosumer environments increasingly adopt:

AI-assisted video editing
Local LLM inference
Multi-device gaming over LAN
Cloud-mirrored data pipelines

To explore current NAS offerings, buyers can browse Newegg’s NAS category for a broad selection.

Choosing the Right 10GbE NAS for Your Use Case

Selecting the right system depends heavily on workload type, required storage capacity, physical space constraints, and budget. Newegg supports multiple form factors, each designed for a different environment.

1. Desktop NAS for Creative Studios & Gaming Homes

Desktop NAS units provide a balance of performance and convenience. They fit neatly into office or gaming desk setups and support both HDD and SSD configurations.

A robust checklist for selecting a desktop NAS includes:

Multi-core CPU (e.g., Intel Celeron, AMD Ryzen)
NVMe SSD caching for fast project loading
At least one native 10GbE port
Expandable drive bays for long-term growth

To review suitable units, the Desktop NAS section offers various models optimized for small studios and high-performance home use.

2. Rackmount NAS for Prosumer Labs and Production Teams

Media studios and advanced home labs often require more robust thermal design, higher drive counts, and redundant components. Rackmount NAS systems address these needs with:

Hot-swap bays
Dual 10GbE ports
ECC memory support
Redundant power supplies

For users considering a rack-based upgrade, the Rackmount NAS catalog outlines scalable enterprise-grade models ideal for long-term growth.

3. Build-Your-Own NAS for Maximum Flexibility

Tech-savvy users may prefer to build a fully customized NAS tailored to specific throughput, caching, and compute requirements. Newegg’s NAS Builder tool guides users through chassis, CPU, memory, and storage selections, ensuring component compatibility and performance alignment.

For those opting for DIY, component choice is critical. You can source essential parts directly:

CPUs: Multi-core processors from the CPU marketplace
Motherboards: NAS-ready boards from the motherboard category
Memory: ECC or high-reliability RAM from Newegg’s RAM offerings
NAS-rated hard drives: High endurance drives from the NAS HDD section
Modern 10GbE NAS Use Cases
1. 4K/8K Video Editing and VFX Workflows

Video professionals increasingly rely on 10GbE to maintain real-time editing performance while working on RAW or ProRes footage. Shared NAS storage reduces the need to move assets between local drives and enables collaborative editing across multiple workstations.

2. AI-Assisted Creative Work

AI-enhanced pipelines—such as video upscaling, 3D model generation, and LLM-based automation—depend on rapid data access. A NAS with SSD caching allows AI models to pull assets with minimal latency.

3. LAN Gaming and High-capacity Game Libraries

Modern titles frequently exceed 100 GB, and managing them across multiple devices leads to duplication and unnecessary storage cost. Hosting a centralized game library on a 10GbE NAS supports:

Fast game loading
Multi-PC access
LAN-party level asset streaming

Buyers expanding into high-performance gaming ecosystems may also explore Newegg’s Gaming PC Finder and Custom PC Builder to configure systems optimized for local 10GbE environments.

Additionally, selecting an appropriate GPU and CPU can significantly boost game streaming and asset indexing performance:

GPUs: Graphics card selection
CPUs: Processor catalog
Key Technologies That Enhance 10GbE NAS Performance
1. NVMe SSD Caching

Caching accelerates data access for frequently used files, dramatically improving gaming and editing responsiveness.

2. Link Aggregation

Combining multiple network ports provides greater throughput and redundancy, ideal for multi-user households.

3. RAID Configurations

Appropriate RAID levels ensure reliable performance and data integrity. Creative professionals frequently deploy RAID 5 or RAID 10 to balance speed and redundancy.

4. Hybrid Storage Architectures

Blending HDD arrays with SSD tiers offers scalability while keeping frequently accessed assets on high-speed media.

Preparing Your Home Network for 10GbE

A fast NAS alone does not guarantee optimal performance. Consider the following upgrades:

10GbE-capable switches
CAT6A or CAT7 cabling
Multi-gig routers
Proper network segmentation for gaming vs media workloads

Investing in these supporting elements ensures the NAS can deliver sustained high throughput across the entire environment.

Conclusion: Building a High-Performance, Future-Ready Home Network

Adopting a 10GbE NAS is one of the most impactful technology upgrades for media professionals, content creators, and demanding gamers. It not only accelerates workflows today but also provides a scalable foundation for emerging technologies—from AI-powered media pipelines to increasingly data-intensive games.

Whether selecting a pre-configured system from the NAS catalog or designing a custom configuration using tools such as NAS Builder, Newegg offers a comprehensive ecosystem to support the transition to next-generation home networking.

With thoughtful planning and the right hardware, any household can build a resilient, high-bandwidth storage environment that remains relevant for years to come.

results.title: Best 8-Bay NAS for Media Libraries and Small Offices | ComputingForGeeks
results.text:
Best 8-Bay NAS for Media Libraries and Small Offices | ComputingForGeeks 
 Skip to content 
 ⓘ This post contains affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Learn more .
 Eight bays is the point where the drives cost more than the NAS. Eight new 16TB WD Red Pro drives come to about $5,700. The boxes in this guide run from about $930 to $2,100 diskless, so the drives are 70 to 90 percent of every 16TB total we priced. Pick the 8-bay NAS for its CPU, network and warranty, then budget most of the money for disks.
 Original content from computingforgeeks.com - post 176358 
 We checked every price, seller and spec on October 21, 2026, against the maker spec sheets and the Amazon US listings. This is a spec-verified guide, not a hands-on test. The picks are split into two jobs: a big media library, where Quick Sync and capacity per dollar decide, and a small office, where ECC, ZFS or DSM and warranty length decide. For fewer drives, the 4-bay NAS guide covers the same ground one size down.
 8-bay NAS picks at a glance
 We ranked the six picks by job, with the diskless price band and the total once eight 16TB Red Pro drives are added. Usable space is the same 96 TB in RAID 6 on all of them, so the populated column is the real comparison:
 Pick Best for CPU Network ECC Box With 8x 16TB 
 UGREEN DXP8800 Plus Plex or Jellyfin library Core i5-1235U, Quick Sync 2x 10GbE No $1,350 to $1,400 about $7,100 
 QNAP TS-832PX-4G Cheap bulk storage ARM Alpine AL324 2x 10GbE SFP+, 2x 2.5GbE No $1,100 to $1,150 about $6,800 
 QNAP TS-873A-8G ZFS on a budget Ryzen V1500B 2x 2.5GbE, 10GbE by card Supported, ships non-ECC $1,400 to $1,450 about $7,150 
 Synology DS1825+ Windows and AD office Ryzen V1500B 2x 2.5GbE, 10GbE by card Yes $1,450 to $1,500 about $7,200 
 Synology DS1823xs+ Business-critical, 5-year warranty Ryzen V1780B 10GbE + 2x 1GbE Yes $2,000 to $2,100 about $7,750 
 UniFi UNAS Pro 8 Rack in a UniFi network 4-core ARM Cortex-A57 2x 10G SFP+, 1x 10GbE No $930 to $960 about $6,650 
 Box prices differ by about $1,100 from the cheapest to the dearest. The spread between eight 12TB and eight 20TB drives is about $2,800, which is why the next section prices the drives before the box. All prices move during the 2026 shortage, so check the current price on Amazon before you order.
 How the numbers were collected
 Nothing here was benchmarked in our lab, so every figure has a source behind it. Each method below states where its numbers came from, and the sources file for this guide lists every page:
 Prices and sellers: the Amazon affiliate API on October 21, 2026, then a second check of the live product page with a US address, because the seller the API reports and the seller on the page disagreed for one pick.
 Specs: the maker spec page or datasheet first, then an independent review (ServeTheHome, NASCompares, ITPro, How-To Geek) where one exists.
 Usable capacity: RAID 6 keeps six of eight drives for data. The RAIDZ2 figure is 71.0 percent of raw, from the 8-wide row in our measured RAIDZ2 width table.
 Rebuild time: a floor computed as drive capacity divided by the maximum transfer rate in the WD datasheet, not a measured rebuild.
 Power figures are the makers’ own unless the text names a review, and not every maker says whether drives were fitted. The TS-832PX has no independent review at all, and the text says so where it matters.
 Step 1: Price the drives before the box
 New drives sold by Amazon itself came only from WD on the check date. Every new Seagate IronWolf Pro listing was a third-party seller with thin stock, and every Exos below $700 was renewed or recertified:
 Drive Per drive 8 drives RAID 6 usable Per usable TB 
 WD Red Pro 12TB $520 to $560 about $4,300 72 TB about $60 
 WD Red Pro 16TB $700 to $730 about $5,700 96 TB about $60 
 WD Red Pro 20TB $870 to $910 about $7,100 120 TB about $59 
 Seagate Exos X18 16TB, recertified $490 to $510 about $4,000 96 TB about $42 
 Cost per usable terabyte is nearly flat across the new Red Pro sizes: about $60 at 12TB and $59 at 20TB. Buy the capacity you need and not the size that looks cheaper per terabyte. The 12TB Red Pro is an air-filled drive rated at 34 dBA idle. The 16TB and 20TB helium models are rated at 20 dBA and draw 3.6 W idle against 6.1 W. In an office or under a desk, that makes 16TB the quieter floor.
 WD rates Red Plus for up to 8 bays and Red Pro for any bay count, so a full 8-bay box sits at the Red Plus ceiling. Red Plus is allowed, but Red Pro is the default we would buy for a box that runs office workloads around the clock. Our NAS hard drive guide ranks both by price per terabyte. Every drive here is CMR, which matters for the reasons in our CMR vs SMR explainer .
 Recertified drives cut the drive bill by about $1,700 on eight 16TB units. The trade is the warranty: the goHardDrive listing quotes a six-month Seagate replacement warranty, against five years on a new Red Pro. Our recertified drive guide covers when that trade makes sense, and a parity array with a second copy of the data is the case it fits.
 Step 2: Size the array for RAID 6 or RAIDZ2
 At eight drives of 12TB or more, RAID 6 or RAIDZ2 is the layout to run, because a rebuild reads every surviving drive end to end. The floor for that read, from the transfer rates WD rates them at, is half a day or more:
 Drive Rated max rate Rebuild floor RAID 6 usable RAIDZ2 reported 
 WD Red Pro 12TB 267 MB/s 12.5 h 72 TB (65.5 TiB) 68.2 TB 
 WD Red Pro 16TB 259 MB/s 17.2 h 96 TB (87.3 TiB) 90.9 TB 
 WD Red Pro 20TB 285 MB/s 19.5 h 120 TB (109.1 TiB) 113.6 TB 
 These floors assume the outer-track rate for the whole drive and no load from users, so real rebuilds run longer. A single-parity array spends that whole rebuild one drive failure from losing everything, which is the case against RAID 5 at these sizes.
 RAIDZ2 reports less space than RAID 6 for the same eight drives, 113.6 TB against 120 TB on 20TB disks, because of ZFS padding and the slop space ZFS reserves at the default record size. The full width table is in our RAIDZ2 drive count guide , where eight is also the widest vdev a single 8-port HBA can run.
 Eight 20TB drives also hit a Synology limit. Both Synology datasheets say a volume over 108 TB needs 32 GB of memory or more, and both boxes ship with 8 GB. A single 120 TB RAID 6 volume on either one means raising the RAM to its 32 GB maximum, or splitting the pool into two volumes.
 Step 3: Choose a box for a big media library
 A media library needs hardware transcoding for remote streams, enough network to move large files, and the lowest box price that still does both. Only one current desktop 8-bay box under $1,500 has an Intel iGPU with Quick Sync.
 UGREEN NASync DXP8800 Plus
 UGREEN NASync DXP8800 Plus. About $1,350 to $1,400; check the current price on Amazon. 
 The DXP8800 Plus runs a 10-core Core i5-1235U with Iris Xe graphics, which gives it Quick Sync for Plex and Jellyfin. It ships with 8 GB of DDR5 (64 GB maximum), two 10GbE ports, two Thunderbolt 4 ports, two NVMe slots, a PCIe x4 slot and a 128 GB boot SSD. UGREEN rates it at 70.39 W in access and 28.99 W with the drives hibernated, and sells it on Amazon itself.
 Drives: third-party drives are supported, with a compatibility list but no lock.
 Other operating systems: the UGREEN warranty page says the hardware warranty stays unchanged if you install a third-party system, which is why it is a common TrueNAS and Unraid box.
 Memory: the DDR5 is on-die ECC only. Intel lists no ECC support for the CPU, so this is not an ECC NAS.
 Warranty: 3 years under the UGREEN warranty policy, even though one block on the product page shows 2.
 Skip it if the data needs true ECC or a mature business suite. It is already the high-capacity pick in our Plex and Jellyfin NAS guide . The DXP Ultra guide covers the DXP8800 Ultra at about $1,750 to $1,800, which changes the CPU and the RAM ceiling (96 GB) and little else.
 QNAP TS-832PX-4G
 QNAP TS-832PX-4G. About $1,100 to $1,150; check the current price on Amazon. 
 The TS-832PX is the cheapest desktop 8-bay box with 10GbE built in, with two 10GbE SFP+ ports and two 2.5GbE ports. Amazon sold it at about $1,100 to $1,150, with five left on the check date. QNAP rates it at 50.9 W typical and 27.9 W in standby with drives fitted.
 The CPU is a 4-core ARM Alpine AL324 at 1.7 GHz with 4 GB of non-ECC RAM in one slot (16 GB maximum), and it runs QTS only. That limits it to serving files: no transcoding, no ZFS, and little room for containers or VMs. Its single PCIe slot is Gen2 x2, and QNAP itself notes that a card there will restrict 10GbE performance. The warranty is 2 years, against 3 on the UGREEN, DS1825+ and TS-873A and 5 on the DS1823xs+. We also found no independent review of it. We kept it as a pick anyway. QNAP publishes full specs and power figures, and it is the only desktop 8-bay with 10GbE at this price.
 Anything on the box that needs a CPU rules it out. Buy it as a backup target or a bulk media share whose players do their own decoding.
 Step 4: Choose a box for a small office
 An office box is judged on what happens when something fails: ECC memory, a file system with snapshots, a warranty that covers the service life, and a supported upgrade path to 10GbE. Four picks cover that, from a budget ZFS box to a rack unit for UniFi sites.
 QNAP TS-873A-8G
 QNAP TS-873A-8G. About $1,400 to $1,450; check the current price on Amazon. 
 The TS-873A is the cheapest pick here with ZFS and an ECC-capable CPU. It runs a 4-core Ryzen Embedded V1500B with 8 GB of RAM (64 GB maximum). It boots QTS or QuTS hero, the QNAP ZFS system with snapshots and inline compression. Two PCIe Gen3 x4 slots take a 10GbE card and a second card; the onboard ports are two 2.5GbE.
 ServeTheHome measured 26 W idle with no drives and a 58 W maximum in its 2021 review, and QNAP rates it at 54.1 W typical with drives. The platform dates from 2021, and its two M.2 slots are Gen3 x1, so NVMe cache is slow. The stock 8 GB is not ECC. QNAP says ECC memory requires removing the pre-installed modules, because ECC and non-ECC cannot be mixed, so matched ECC SODIMMs are an extra cost on top of the box price. Price a 10GbE card from the QNAP compatibility list in from the start too, and plan for 16 GB of RAM for ZFS deduplication; ITPro recommends 32 GB for QuTS hero once 10GbE is added.
 Look elsewhere if you want ECC or 10GbE without extra parts, or fast M.2 storage.
 Synology DS1825+
 Synology DS1825+. About $1,450 to $1,500; check the current price and seller on Amazon. 
 The DS1825+ is the pick for an office that already runs Active Directory and wants DSM. It has the same Ryzen V1500B as the TS-873A, with 8 GB of ECC DDR4 (32 GB maximum) and two 2.5GbE ports. Two NVMe slots and a PCIe Gen3 slot with an x4 link for a 10GbE or 25GbE card complete it. Two DX525 expansion units take it to 18 bays, and Synology rates it at 60.1 W in access.
 On DSM 7.3 or later, the 2025 Plus models accept unlisted hard drives for new pools again. Unlisted M.2 drives are still limited to migration, with no new pool or cache, so buy Synology SSDs if you want NVMe cache. The full policy is on the Synology drive compatibility page , and our Synology alternative guide compares it with the other vendors.
 On the check date, the page seller was RockyStone Electronics, a third party, at about $1,450 to $1,500. The Amazon catalogue listed Amazon as the merchant at the same time. Check who sells it before you order, and buy from an authorized Synology reseller if warranty support matters. Our small business NAS guide covers the DSM and AD setup, and the neo+ vs Plus comparison covers the cheaper DS1825neo+.
 Synology DS1823xs+
 Synology DS1823xs+. About $2,000 to $2,100; check the current price on Amazon. 
 About $600 more than the DS1825+ buys three things: a 5-year warranty, a faster 4-core Ryzen V1780B, and 10GbE on the board next to two 1GbE ports and a management port. It has 8 GB of ECC memory (32 GB maximum), the same Gen3 slot with an x4 link, and 18 bays with two DX517 units. Synology rates it at 87.93 W in access. Amazon sells it directly.
 As a 2023 xs model, it is outside the 2025 drive policy change, because Synology says that change does not apply retroactively. Owners report “unverified” warnings in DSM when they fit third-party drives. It also has no SHR, only standard RAID levels.
 Pass on it if you plan to fill it with WD or Seagate drives and do not want those warnings, or if anything needs transcoding.
 UniFi UNAS Pro 8
 UniFi UNAS Pro 8. About $930 to $960 from a third-party seller on Amazon; check the current price. 
 UniFi built the cheapest box here and the only rack unit among the picks: 2U, 480 mm deep, with rails in the box. It has two 10G SFP+ ports and one 10GbE RJ45 port, a 4-core ARM Cortex-A57 with 16 GB of soldered RAM, and two hot-swap power supply bays. NASCompares measured about 800 to 850 MB/s sequential read from eight 8TB drives in RAID 5.
 Price: Ubiquiti lists it at about $800 before a checkout surcharge. On Amazon it comes from a third-party seller at about $930 to $960 on October 21, 2026; check the current price.
 Power: one 550 W supply is included, and the second for redundancy costs about $159.
 Storage: RAID 5, 6 or 10 with a hot spare, shared over SMB and NFS. There is no iSCSI and no app or container platform, and the trays for its two M.2 cache slots are sold separately.
 Warranty: the UI Store page lists no base term, only UI Care, which extends cover to 5 years for about $199. US resellers list a 1-year limited warranty, which would make it the shortest base cover here.
 Skip it if you need Docker, iSCSI, ECC or any software outside UniFi Drive. Buy it if the rack already holds UniFi gear; our first rackmount server guide covers depth and rails for a home rack.
 Step 5: Price a DIY 8-bay build
 A DIY build with Quick Sync and eight SATA ports on the board costs about the same as the DXP8800 Plus at current DDR5 prices. This basket uses a Jonsbo N3 case and a Mini-ITX board with eight SATA ports, so no HBA is needed:
 Part Pick Band 
 Case Jonsbo N3, 8 hot-swap bays about $160 
 Board StoneStorm Q670 Mini-ITX, 8 SATA about $210 
 CPU Intel Core i5-14400 about $210 
 Memory Crucial Pro 2×16 GB DDR5-6000 about $540 
 Power Cooler Master V750 SFX Gold about $125 
 Boot WD Green SN3000 500 GB about $95 
 10GbE TP-Link TX401 about $60 
 We priced the basket at about $1,400 for 32 GB of RAM, against 8 GB in the DXP8800 Plus at about the same price. A lean version with 16 GB and a Core i3-14100 comes to about $1,050 to $1,100, though the i3 was listed for a later ship date. Several parts were sold by third parties with thin stock. The specs for the board come from its Amazon listing only, and that listing does not state the PCIe slot, so confirm it before you buy the 10GbE card.
 DIY no longer saves money at this size, so build one for the freedom to run any OS. Unraid at eight drives also needs its Unleashed licence, about $109, on top of the basket. There is also no ECC on a Q670 board. The case options are in our NAS case guide , the power and cost comparison is in DIY NAS vs prebuilt , and the OS choice is in TrueNAS vs Unraid .
 Step 6: Match the network to the array
 Eight hard drives in a parity array read faster than a 2.5GbE port can carry. NASCompares measured 800 to 850 MB/s from eight 8TB drives in RAID 5 on the UNAS Pro 8. A 2.5GbE link tops out near 280 MB/s, so a 2.5GbE-only box leaves most of the array idle on large transfers.
 10GbE on the board: DXP8800 Plus, TS-832PX, DS1823xs+ and UNAS Pro 8. On the DXP8800 Ultra, ITPro measured 9.2 Gbit/s read and 8.8 Gbit/s write in the Iometer synthetic test, and 3.8 and 3.0 Gbit/s copying a 25 GB file.
 10GbE by card: TS-873A and DS1825+. Use a card from the QNAP or Synology compatibility list for each box.
 The switch: a 10GbE NAS needs a 10GbE port at the other end, which our 10GbE switch guide covers.
 A 1GbE or 2.5GbE network is fine for streaming, because a single 4K stream needs a small fraction of either. The 10GbE port pays off on backups, video editing and VM storage, and the box belongs on a UPS whichever network it runs, as our NAS UPS guide explains.
 Models we left out and why
 Several 8-bay boxes looked right in a search and failed a check. Each one is excluded for a specific, verifiable reason:
 QNAP TS-855X: the Amazon title says 8 bays, but the box has six 3.5-inch bays and two 2.5-inch bays.
 Synology DS1821+: discontinued. Its US product page now redirects to the download center, and the remaining Amazon listings are third-party bundles above $3,700.
 Asustor Lockerstor 8 Gen3 (AS6808T): true ECC and 10GbE, but about $1,820 or more everywhere, third-party only on Amazon, and no written independent review.
 TerraMaster U8-500 Plus: a 2U unit with a Core i7-1255U and 10GbE at about $1,530, but no independent review we could find, and its RAID grows only by swapping in larger drives, not by adding drives.
 TerraMaster U8-423: a 2U unit with a Celeron N5095 that does hardware transcoding, two 2.5GbE ports and a 2-year warranty, at about $825 direct from TerraMaster but not sold on Amazon US.
 TerraMaster F8 SSD: all-flash, covered in our all-flash NAS guide .
 QNAP TVS-h874 and TS-855eU: out of stock or used only on the check date.
 QNAP also previewed an 8-bay AI NAS at Computex in June 2026 without US availability, so it is not in this guide until it ships. Past eight drives, the next step is an expansion unit or a DAS or JBOD enclosure , not a bigger NAS.
