 Factors to Consider When Choosing Network Attached Storage For Gaming Library
Choosing the right NAS for your gaming library involves several key factors. Understanding these will help you avoid common pitfalls, such as overpaying for unnecessary features or underestimating storage needs. The right balance of speed, capacity, and ease of use depends heavily on your specific gaming habits and technical comfort level. Carefully considering these factors ensures you pick a device that offers smooth gameplay, quick access, and future-proofing for expanding libraries. Performance and Network Speed
 For gaming libraries, network speed is essential. Look for NAS units supporting 10GbE or higher if you want fast game launches and seamless streaming, especially with multiple users. A powerful processor ensures that the NAS can handle simultaneous access and data transfers without lag. Cheaper models may only support 1GbE, which can become a bottleneck during intensive gaming sessions or media streaming, leading to frustrating delays. Capacity and Expandability
 Gaming libraries can grow quickly, so capacity is a key consideration. Decide whether you prefer a diskless model, which gives flexibility to choose drives, or pre-populated ones for immediate use. Larger capacity units with multiple bays allow future expansion, but they often come at a higher cost. Consider your current library size and expected growth, and choose a device that balances storage needs with budget constraints. Ease of Use and Management
 User-friendly interfaces and straightforward setup processes are especially important if you’re not highly technical. Brands like Synology are known for intuitive software that simplifies management, remote access, and backups. Conversely, more advanced models with extensive features can be overwhelming for beginners, potentially leading to configuration errors or underutilization of capabilities. Hardware Features and Transcoding
 Features such as hardware transcoding, M.2 NVMe slots, and HDMI output can enhance your gaming experience—enabling real-time game streaming or media playback directly from the NAS. However, these features often increase the cost and complexity. Evaluate whether your gaming setup truly benefits from these extras, or if they are unnecessary for your use case. Build Quality and Support
 Durability and warranty support can influence long-term satisfaction, particularly if your NAS will be running continuously. Devices with solid build quality and responsive customer service reduce downtime and maintenance hassles. Investing in a reputable brand or a device with a good warranty can save money and frustration down the line, especially for intensive gaming workloads. Frequently Asked Questions
 How much capacity do I need for my gaming library?
 The required capacity depends on your current library size and future growth plans. If you have hundreds of games, especially large AAA titles, opting for a 4-bay NAS with multiple drive bays or pre-populated large drives makes sense. For casual gamers with a smaller collection, a 2-bay unit might suffice, but remember to leave room for expansion as your library grows. Always choose a device that can accommodate your expected needs without forcing costly upgrades later. Is a 10GbE network necessary for gaming?
 While a 10GbE connection isn’t strictly necessary for casual gaming, it becomes valuable if you want fast load times and smooth streaming for large files or multiple users. For single-user setups or smaller libraries, gigabit Ethernet may be adequate. However, investing in 10GbE support future-proofs your setup and minimizes bottlenecks, especially if you plan to expand or run multiple devices simultaneously. Should I prioritize hardware transcoding features?
 Hardware transcoding can enhance your media streaming experience, especially if you plan to stream games or media to multiple devices. However, for purely local gaming libraries, transcoding offers limited benefits. It’s more beneficial if you also intend to use the NAS for media serving or live game streaming, but be aware that these features often add to the cost and complexity of setup. Are diskless NAS units a good choice?
 Diskless units offer flexibility, allowing you to choose and upgrade drives as needed. This can be more cost-effective initially and lets you tailor storage to your specific needs. However, the process of purchasing compatible drives and setting up RAID or other configurations can be intimidating for beginners. If you prefer plug-and-play simplicity, pre-configured drives might be a better option, even if they cost a bit more upfront. How important is build quality for a gaming NAS?
 Build quality impacts the device’s durability and reliability, especially if it will run 24/7. Cheaper, poorly made NAS units may overheat or fail prematurely, risking data loss or downtime during gaming sessions. Selecting a model from a reputable manufacturer with solid construction and good warranty support helps ensure your gaming library remains accessible and safe over the long term. Conclusion
 For most users, the Ugreen NAS DXP4800 GT offers an excellent balance of performance, expandability, and features, making it the best overall choice. Budget-conscious gamers or newcomers will find the Synology DS223 straightforward and reliable, ideal for starting small without sacrificing future growth. Those seeking premium features, like hardware transcoding and HDMI output, should consider the UGREEN NAS DXP4800 Plus or ACEMAGIC NAS N3A . Ultimately, your selection should align with your current library size, technical comfort, and future plans—making sure you pick a device that genuinely enhances your gaming experience now and later.

 We prioritized models that combine 10GbE networking with strong CPU and memory options, enough drive bays for sensible growth, and features that matter in real use such as NVMe cache, SSD support, or expansion flexibility. We also looked for clear fit across home media servers, creator workstations, and small-business file sharing.
 Quick Comparison 
 The best 10GbE NAS enclosures in this roundup generally fall into three groups: compact desktop units for home and creator setups, higher-bay systems for teams and larger libraries, and rackmount options for structured deployments. More bays usually mean more capacity and better RAID flexibility, while faster CPUs and more RAM help with containers, virtualization, and multiple simultaneous users.
 Key Buying Factors for a Nas Enclosure with 10gbe 
 Drive Bays and Storage Growth
 Choose bay count based on both current needs and future expansion. Four-bay models suit many personal and creator workloads, six-bay units add more flexibility for RAID and larger media libraries, and eight-bay enclosures are better if you expect rapid growth or want more redundancy.
 CPU, RAM, and Workload Type
 A basic file server needs less processing power than a system running Plex, Docker, machine learning tools, or multiple users. For a Nas Enclosure with 10gbe, pair the network speed with enough CPU headroom and memory so the system does not become a bottleneck.
 Storage Mix and Cache Options
 Some enclosures support only HDDs, while others add SSD or NVMe slots for cache or all-flash arrays. SSD-heavy or hybrid designs can improve responsiveness for active projects, databases, and frequently accessed files.
 Ports and Connectivity
 Look beyond 10GbE alone. Extra USB ports, additional LAN ports, and expansion support can make backups, peripherals, and future networking simpler. If your switch or workstation is not ready for 10GbE, verify compatibility and the required cabling before buying.
 Who Should Buy Which Nas Enclosure with 10gbe? 
 Choose a compact 4-bay unit if you want fast shared storage for a single user, a couple of creators, or a home lab. Step up to a 6-bay model if you need better growth room for media, business files, or mixed workloads. Pick an 8-bay system if capacity, redundancy, and long-term expansion matter most. For office or rack-based setups, a rackmount enclosure is the cleanest fit.
 In short, the right choice depends on whether you value speed, capacity, or flexibility most. Match the enclosure to your workload, then use 10GbE to remove the network bottleneck and keep your storage feeling fast.

 How We Picked
 I compared these systems by how directly they serve a 10GbE storage workflow: native network speed and port count came first, followed by bay capacity, processor and memory headroom, expansion options, and the work needed to set up and maintain the system. For buyers moving large files or serving several clients, dual 10GbE and room for enough drives can matter more than headline processor specifications. I also weighed whether a product is diskless or arrives with storage, since that changes the setup and upgrade decision.
 The ranking favors systems with clearly stated 10GbE connectivity and useful storage capacity. The QNAP leads for its combination of dual 10GbE and nine bays, while the DXP8800 Plus earns a strong position through its eight-bay design and current hardware. Models with 1GbE are included because they appear in the requested lineup, but they rank as alternatives for buyers who may not need 10GbE immediately; they cannot substitute for a native 10GbE NAS when that connection is mandatory.  Factors to Consider When Choosing 10gbe Nas
 Choosing a 10GbE NAS means planning a storage system, not just selecting a fast network port. I would start with the workload and the clients that need access, then match drive capacity, network equipment, and setup effort to those needs.
 Check the Whole Network Path
 A 10GbE NAS can communicate at that link speed only when the client and every relevant network connection support it. Check whether your computer has a 10GbE port, whether your switch supports the speed, and whether the cabling and adapters are suitable. A direct connection between one computer and the NAS can avoid buying a multiport switch, but it may complicate access for other devices. If only one workstation moves large files, a direct link may be a practical starting point. For several users, plan the switch and uplinks before choosing port count. Otherwise, you may pay for NAS networking capacity that the rest of the setup cannot use.
 Estimate Capacity and Drive Redundancy
 Count the usable storage you need after accounting for redundancy, snapshots, and growth, rather than adding up the drive labels. More bays can let you combine larger capacity with redundancy or add drives over time, but extra bays also mean more drives to buy, monitor, and replace. Two-bay systems are simpler to place and manage, yet leave fewer options for capacity and drive layouts. Do not assume a RAID configuration replaces a separate backup; it mainly helps keep a system available when a drive fails. For important files, budget for a backup destination or cloud copy as part of the storage plan. Choosing too few bays early can make later expansion more disruptive.
 Match Drives and Workload to Throughput
 The network port sets a ceiling, while the drives and workload determine how close transfers get to it. A single hard drive will not usually saturate a 10GbE link, and many small-file operations behave differently from a large video transfer. SSDs, caching, and parallel drive access can help with particular workloads, but they add cost, heat, and maintenance choices. Decide whether your bottleneck is sequential transfer speed, concurrent users, or application processing before paying for flash storage or a faster CPU. For media editing, check the workflow from source drive through NAS to client, including the software and file sizes involved. For backups and archives, capacity and reliability may matter more than peak transfer rates.
 Compare Expansion and Compatibility
 Expansion features only help when they fit equipment you own or plan to use. M.2 slots may support cache, storage, or both depending on the system, so verify the intended role instead of assuming every slot adds usable capacity. USB4, OCuLink, and HDMI can suit specialized workflows, but they do not improve ordinary NAS file access by themselves. Check supported drive sizes, memory limits, and whether parts can be replaced before committing to a diskless system. Also confirm that the operating system supports the backup, container, or media services you plan to run. A simpler configuration can be easier to maintain than a highly expandable one if your storage needs are stable.
 Choose a Setup and Maintenance Style
 Diskless NAS systems give you control over drive selection, but you must choose compatible drives, install them, create storage pools, and plan backups. A preconfigured package can reduce initial setup, though it may offer less choice over the included components and later changes. Before buying, look at how the vendor handles software updates, drive health alerts, account security, and recovery after a hardware failure. Consider who will administer the NAS after setup, especially in a small office where the original buyer may not be available. A beginner-friendly interface can save time, while a system that allows more customization may suit someone comfortable managing services. Choose for the maintenance routine you can sustain, not only the initial installation.
 Decide Whether Native 10GbE Is Required Now
 Not every buyer needs 10GbE on day one, but a NAS with 1GbE will not provide a native 10GbE connection just because the rest of the network is upgraded. If your current work involves ordinary backups and shared documents, a lower-speed system may be adequate while you plan a future network change. For frequent large project transfers or multiple high-speed clients, prioritize a model whose stated ports meet the requirement. Confirm whether the NAS has one or two 10GbE ports and how you intend to use them; dual ports do not automatically double the speed of one client connection. This roundup includes several 1GbE models, so treat them as slower-network alternatives rather than direct 10GbE replacements. Buying for a future upgrade makes sense only if the system itself can support that upgrade.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Will a 10GbE NAS make my file transfers ten times faster?
 No. The 10GbE link offers more network capacity than a 1GbE link, but actual transfer speed also depends on the NAS drives, RAID configuration, client hardware, protocol, and file type. Large sequential files are more likely to benefit than folders full of small files. A single hard drive may become the limit before the network does. Check the slowest part of your current workflow before upgrading.
 Do I need a 10GbE switch if my NAS has two 10GbE ports?
 Not always. A direct cable connection can link a single 10GbE computer and NAS without a switch, though network setup may take extra configuration and other devices will still need a separate path. A switch is more useful when several computers need fast access or when the NAS must join a larger network. Two NAS ports do not automatically give one client twice the speed; the client, protocol, and workload must support the arrangement. Plan around the number of devices that need high-speed access.
 Can a NAS with 1GbE work with a 10GbE network?
 It can connect to a faster network, but its 1GbE port remains the limiting link for NAS traffic. That makes the listed UGREEN DH2300 and the two-bay DXP2800 models poor matches if native 10GbE transfers are a firm requirement. They may still suit backups or shared files where 1GbE is adequate. If you expect to upgrade later, confirm whether the NAS supports a network card or another path to 10GbE instead of assuming one can be added.
 Is a diskless NAS a better choice than a preconfigured system?
 A diskless system gives you control over drive models, capacity, and how you build the storage pool, but you take on compatibility checks and setup. A preconfigured package can get you started with storage already included, while limiting your choices about those drives. Neither approach removes the need for a separate backup plan. Compare the included components, supported drive list, and replacement process before deciding. The right fit depends on whether you value configuration control or a simpler initial setup.
 Should I choose more bays or an all-flash NAS for video work?
 It depends on whether your limiting factor is capacity or the speed of active project files. More bays can provide ample space for a large media library and multiple drives, while an all-flash design can suit smaller, frequently accessed working sets. Neither choice guarantees smooth editing; client connectivity, network layout, codecs, and simultaneous users matter too. Many workflows use fast storage for active projects and larger-capacity storage for archives. Estimate active project size and transfer patterns before choosing between capacity and flash performance.
 Conclusion
 For a broad mix of fast transfers and expandable storage, I would start with the QNAP TS-932PX-4G as the best overall choice, thanks to its dual 10GbE and nine-bay layout. The UGREEN DXP8800 Plus is my pick for buyers who want eight bays and an Intel i5 platform, while the Synology DS1823xs+ is the premium option for those who prefer a business-oriented preconfigured package. For beginners, the UGREEN DH2300 is positioned as an accessible two-bay system, but its 1GbE port makes it unsuitable when 10GbE is essential. For a compact all-flash workflow, consider the UGREEN DXP480T Plus ; for a lower-complexity two-bay alternative, compare the DXP2800 models while checking their networking limits. My key distinction is simple: choose for the network speed you need today, then size bays and drive type around the files and people the NAS will serve.

 How we judged the field
 We do not run our own storage lab. Instead we synthesize published reviews and aggregated owner reports to reach a verdict you can trust. For home NAS units in the 2-to-4-bay class, a handful of criteria consistently separate a great buy from a frustrating one.
 Transcoding ability: whether the processor can hardware-transcode 4K video for Plex, Jellyfin or Emby, which is the single biggest differentiator for media use.
 Networking: 2.5GbE is now the floor; 10GbE is the meaningful upgrade for editing large files over the network.
 Software maturity: how polished, reliable and well-supported the operating system and mobile apps are, which matters most for non-technical households.
 Expansion and memory: NVMe cache slots, memory headroom, and upgrade paths that keep the unit useful for years.
 Drive freedom and value: whether you can use the drives you want, and how much hardware you get for the money. Remember that all of these ship without drives.
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus
 Buy it 
 UGREEN is the newcomer that changed the math. The DXP4800 Plus pairs a 12th-generation Intel Pentium Gold 8505 with 8GB of DDR5 (expandable to 64GB), two NVMe slots, and, crucially, both a 10GbE and a 2.5GbE port. Its integrated graphics with Quick Sync are built for hardware 4K transcoding, and reviewers repeatedly note it undercuts comparable incumbent units by a wide margin. The catch is software: UGOS Pro is improving fast but is younger and has a thinner app ecosystem than DSM. For buyers who prioritize hardware and networking, that is an easy trade to make.
 TerraMaster F4-424 Pro
 Buy it 
 The F4-424 Pro is the horsepower-per-dollar pick. Its eight-core Intel Core i3-N305 with integrated graphics is, by owner and reviewer accounts, among the most capable media-class transcoding chips at its price, and 32GB of DDR5 shipped in the box (the supported maximum) plus dual NVMe slots make it a genuinely strong container and virtualization host. It sticks to dual 2.5GbE rather than 10GbE, and TOS software is functional rather than delightful, which is why a portion of power users install TrueNAS or Unraid on it instead. If you want maximum compute for the least money and do not mind a bit of tinkering, it is an excellent buy.
 Synology DiskStation DS925+
 It depends 
 Synology still makes the software everyone else is chasing. DSM is the most polished and dependable NAS operating system, its backup, Drive, Docker, Virtual Machine Manager and Surveillance Station apps are excellent, and the DS925+ adds ECC memory, dual 2.5GbE and two NVMe slots. The problem is the hardware fit: its AMD Ryzen V1500B has no integrated GPU, so it cannot hardware-transcode video, making it a weak choice for 4K media streaming. Layer on premium pricing and the 2025-generation drive-compatibility saga, and it becomes a conditional recommendation. If you want a rock-solid appliance for backups and apps and do not care about transcoding, it is superb; if media streaming is your goal, look elsewhere.
 QNAP TS-464
 Skip it 
 The TS-464 was a strong all-rounder, and QTS remains a powerful, feature-dense platform with an optional ZFS-based edition. But in 2026 its Intel Celeron N5095 is 2021-era silicon, and owners increasingly note it is outspecced by newer, cheaper rivals while still commanding a premium price. Add QTS’s cluttered interface and QNAP’s well-documented history of security incidents, which demand diligent patching, and there is little reason for a new buyer to choose it. Existing QNAP owners with accessories to reuse are the exception; everyone else can do better for less.
 Sources 
 Specs in this review come from these pages.
 UGREEN, NASync DXP4800 Plus product page (ai.ugreen.com) 
 TerraMaster, F4-424 Pro product page (terra-master.com) 
 Synology, DiskStation DS925+ product page (synology.com) 
 QNAP, TS-464 product page (qnap.com) 
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus vs TerraMaster F4-424 Pro: which should you buy?
 These are the two strongest units, and both are Intel-based media powerhouses that ship without drives, so the decision comes down to networking and software. The UGREEN wins on connectivity: its 10GbE port is a real advantage if you routinely move large video files or run a fast wired network, and its DDR5 ceiling of 64GB gives it more long-term headroom. The TerraMaster wins on price and raw core count, with an eight-core chip that can edge ahead on heavy parallel transcoding and virtualization workloads.
 Choose the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus if you want the most complete, future-proof package and value fast networking and a slightly more consumer-friendly interface. Choose the TerraMaster F4-424 Pro if you want the best value, are comfortable with less polished software, and do not need 10GbE. Neither choice is a mistake; the UGREEN is simply the more rounded product for most homes.
 What to look for
 Match the CPU to your use: if you want Plex or Jellyfin to stream 4K, insist on an Intel chip with integrated graphics for hardware transcoding, and be wary of GPU-less processors.
 Treat 2.5GbE as the minimum, and consider 10GbE only if the rest of your network and your workflow can actually use it.
 Buy memory and NVMe headroom you can grow into; DDR5 and two cache slots age far better than fixed, soldered configurations.
 Check drive compatibility before you buy, and factor two to four drives into your budget since every unit here is sold diskless.
 Weigh software honestly: DSM is the safest bet for non-technical users, while UGOS, TOS and QTS reward buyers willing to learn a little more.
 Plan an off-site backup regardless of model; a NAS with redundancy protects against a dead drive, not against theft, fire or ransomware.
 Our final take
 The home NAS market has been reshaped by aggressive newcomers, and the buying advice has shifted with it. The UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus is our top pick because it delivers the most hardware, the best networking, and modern transcoding at a price the incumbents have not matched. The TerraMaster F4-424 Pro is the value runner-up for buyers who want compute over connectivity. Synology’s DS925+ is still the reliability and software champion, but its inability to hardware-transcode makes it a considered, conditional choice rather than a default. The QNAP TS-464 is the one to skip in 2026 unless you are already locked into its ecosystem. Whichever you choose, budget for drives and an off-site backup, and you will have a home server that earns its keep for years.
 Questions, answered
 Do these NAS devices come with hard drives? No. Every model here ships diskless, which is standard for this class. You buy two to four 3.5-inch SATA hard drives (or SSDs) separately and install them yourself. Budget for the drives as a meaningful part of the total cost, and where possible buy identical drives so a RAID array is balanced. This is general product information, not a recommendation for your specific setup; check each maker's current compatibility list before purchasing.
 How many bays do I actually need, two or four? A 2-bay unit in a mirrored configuration is plenty for backups and a photo vault, and it is cheaper and quieter. Choose a 4-bay model if you run a large, growing media library, want to stream several 4K files at once, or value more flexible expansion and redundancy. All four units reviewed here are four-bay, which is the sweet spot for a long-lived home server.
 Which of these is best for a Plex or Jellyfin media server? The UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus and TerraMaster F4-424 Pro are the strongest, because their Intel chips include integrated graphics that hardware-transcode 4K video efficiently. The Synology DS925+ is the weakest for this specific job: its AMD processor has no GPU and cannot hardware-transcode, so demanding 4K streams fall back to slower software transcoding.
 What is the Synology drive lock-in issue? Synology's 2025-generation units, including the DS925+, initially restricted full functionality to Synology-branded drives and a short approved list. After criticism, a DSM 7.3 update in late 2025 restored the ability to install the system and create storage pools on non-validated third-party drives on Plus, Value and J series models. Some friction and warning prompts can remain, so if you want maximum drive freedom, the other three brands are more open.
 Is a NAS worth it over a cloud subscription? For most households that store a lot of photos, video and backups, yes. A NAS is a one-time hardware cost (plus drives and electricity) rather than a recurring fee, keeps your data in your own home, and gives you far more space than typical cloud tiers. The trade-off is that you are responsible for setup, updates and an off-site backup copy, since a single NAS is not itself a complete backup strategy.

A network-attached storage (NAS) box used to be a thing only IT hobbyists owned. In 2026 it is closer to a household appliance: a small always-on computer with hard drive bays that stores your files, streams your media, and runs the little services that keep a connected home humming. But "best home NAS" is a trick question, because the right pick depends entirely on what you plan to do with it.

This guide skips the spec-sheet overload and organizes the decision around how real people actually use a NAS at home. We will look at who genuinely needs one, walk through three common scenarios, and name a best pick for each.

Who Needs This?

You probably want a NAS if any of these sound like you. First, you are tired of juggling external USB drives and cloud subscriptions and want one private place for everything. Second, you take a lot of photos and video and have outgrown free cloud tiers. Third, you want to stream your own movie and music collection to TVs and phones around the house without monthly streaming fees. Fourth, you want automatic, redundant backups of multiple computers so a single drive failure never costs you data.

You probably do not need one if you own a single laptop, store little, and are happy paying for a cloud plan. For that life, a USB SSD plus cloud sync is simpler and cheaper. A NAS earns its keep when you have multiple devices, multiple people, or a growing media library. If that is you, browse current models on the Newegg NAS selection to see what fits your budget.

Use-Case Scenarios

Scenario 1: Simple backup and photo vault. You want a reliable, low-effort place to back up two or three computers and offload your phone's photo roll. You are not running heavy apps and you do not stream much. Here, two drive bays in a mirror (RAID 1) are plenty, low power draw matters, and ease of setup beats raw horsepower.

Scenario 2: Plex / Jellyfin media server. You have a movie, TV, and music library and want to stream it to TVs, tablets, and phones, sometimes to several screens at once. The deciding factor is the processor and whether it has hardware transcoding and an HDMI port, plus enough bays to hold a large library that keeps growing.

Scenario 3: Power-user home server. You want to run Docker containers, virtual machines, smart-home dashboards, a personal cloud, and maybe self-hosted apps, all at once. You need a strong CPU, generous and upgradable RAM, fast 2.5GbE or 10GbE networking, and NVMe slots for caching.

Best Pick per Scenario

Best for simple backup: Synology DS224+. This is the friendly entry point. It is a 2-bay unit built around a quad-core Intel Celeron at 2.0 GHz with 2GB of DDR4 (expandable to 6GB). Synology's DSM software is the easiest in the category, and its Active Backup and Photos apps handle exactly the "back up my computers and phone" job this scenario describes. Two bays in RAID 1 give you redundancy without overspending. It is available on Newegg, with MSRP around $370 (commonly sold lower).

Best for media server: UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus. For Plex and Jellyfin, this 4-bay unit punches above its price. It runs an Intel Pentium Gold 8505 (a 5-core 12th-gen chip with quick-sync hardware transcoding), ships with 8GB of DDR5, and crucially pairs one 10GbE port with one 2.5GbE port plus a 4K-capable HDMI output. Four bays support up to roughly 144TB of raw capacity, with two NVMe slots for caching. Expect a price around $620, available on Newegg. If you prefer the most polished media app ecosystem instead, the QNAP TS-464 (quad-core Celeron N5095/N5105, 8GB DDR4, HDMI 2.1, dual 2.5GbE) is a strong alternative, available on Newegg.

Best for power-user home server: Synology DS925+ or TerraMaster F4-424 Pro. If you live in the Synology ecosystem and want rock-solid software for Docker, Virtual Machine Manager, and surveillance, the DS925+ is the pick: a 4-bay unit with a quad-core AMD Ryzen V1500B, 4GB ECC DDR4 expandable to 32GB, dual 2.5GbE, and two M.2 slots. MSRP is about $620, available on Newegg. If you want the most raw compute for the money and are comfortable with TerraMaster's TOS software, the F4-424 Pro is a beast for the class: an 8-core Intel Core i3-N305, 32GB of DDR5, four bays, and dual 2.5GbE, with a US price around $699, available on Newegg. The Synology wins on software polish; the TerraMaster wins on horsepower per dollar.

The Drives Matter Too

Whichever enclosure you choose, remember that most home NAS units ship diskless, so you buy the hard drives separately. For an always-on box, use drives rated for 24/7 NAS duty rather than standard desktop drives. You can compare capacities and warranties across the Newegg NAS hard drive selection and plan to fill at least two bays so you can run a mirror from day one.

Verdict

There is no single best home NAS for 2026, only the best one for your scenario. If you just want painless backups and a private photo library, the Synology DS224+ is the easy, affordable answer. If your home revolves around streaming your own media, the UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus delivers transcoding muscle and fast networking at a fair price. And if you are the household tinkerer running containers and virtual machines, step up to the Synology DS925+ for software polish or the TerraMaster F4-424 Pro for sheer performance. Match the box to the job, add NAS-rated drives, and you will have a private cloud that pays for itself in a year or two.

Frequently Asked Questions

Common questions about choosing a home NAS in 2026.

Do I really need a NAS at home?
A NAS is worth it if you have multiple devices or people, a growing photo and video library, or want automatic redundant backups and private media streaming. If you own a single laptop and are happy with a cloud plan, a USB SSD plus cloud sync is simpler and cheaper.
How many drive bays should a home NAS have?
Which NAS is best for Plex in 2026?
Do NAS units come with hard drives?

 Buying Guide – How to Choose the Best 10GbE NAS
 Selecting the right 10GbE NAS requires balancing processor power, storage capacity, and expansion needs. This guide breaks down the critical factors to ensure you buy a device that meets your performance demands.
 Processor Performance
 The processor determines how well your NAS handles tasks like virtualization and media transcoding. Look for Intel Core or AMD Ryzen chips for heavy workflows.
 Prioritize processors with multiple cores and threads to ensure smooth multitasking.
 Network Connectivity
 Ensure the NAS supports at least one 10GbE port for high-speed data transfer. Dual ports allow link aggregation for even higher bandwidth.
 Check if the device has additional 2.5GbE or 1GbE ports for flexible connectivity.
 Storage Capacity
 Calculate your total storage needs based on your media and file library size. Some models support up to 200TB capacity while others are limited.
 Choose a unit with extra drive bays for future growth without replacing the device.
 Memory and RAM
 RAM is crucial for virtual machines and running multiple apps simultaneously. Look for systems that support DDR5 or high-capacity DDR4.
 Opt for expandable RAM options to boost performance over time.
 Operating System
 The OS determines the user experience and available features like Docker support. UGOS Pro offers a clean interface suitable for beginners and pros.
 Choose an OS that supports the apps you need such as Plex or Home Assistant.
 Data Security
 Encryption and RAID support are essential for protecting your local data. Look for built-in security managers and support for TLS/SSL encryption.
 Ensure the device offers robust user permissions and backup features.
 Connectivity Options
 USB and HDMI ports allow direct backups and media playback without a computer. Check for USB 3.2 or Thunderbolt support for external drive speed.
 USB-C and HDMI enable versatile connections for modern devices.
 Expansion and Upgrades
 Some NAS units allow PCIe expansion for adding more network cards or GPUs. This future-proofs your investment against changing needs.
 Verify if M.2 slots are available for SSD caching to improve system speed.
 How to Use and Care for Your 10GbE NAS
 Begin by setting up your network connection with a Cat6a or Cat7 cable to ensure 10GbE speeds. Install the drives and configure RAID settings according to your data protection needs.
 Regularly update the firmware to maintain security and access new features. Use the included apps to manage backups and monitor system health remotely.
 Keep the device in a well-ventilated area to prevent overheating during continuous operation. Clean dust from the vents periodically to maintain optimal airflow.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Do I need a 10GbE router for this NAS? 
 Yes to fully utilize the 10GbE speed your router or switch must support 10-gigabit Ethernet. If not the NAS will still work at standard speeds but you will not get the full transfer performance.
 Can I use this NAS for video editing? 
 Absolutely the 10GbE connection allows for smooth playback and editing of 4K video directly from the device. This is ideal for creators and professionals needing fast access.
 What happens if a hard drive fails? 
 If you configure RAID 1 or 5 the data remains safe even if one drive fails. You can replace the failed drive and rebuild the array without losing your files.
 Is the NAS cloud accessible? 
 Most modern NAS devices allow remote access via secure apps. You can access files from anywhere using a browser or mobile app with proper setup.
 How do I expand storage later? 
 Choose a model with extra drive bays or support for expansion units. Some devices allow adding external USB drives or M.2 SSDs for more space.
 Do these NAS units run 24/7? 
 Yes they are designed for continuous operation. Efficient cooling systems and hardware ensure stable performance even during constant read and write cycles.
 Can I run servers on this NAS? 
 Many models support Docker containers and virtual machines allowing you to run servers like Plex or Home Assistant locally. This turns your storage into a powerful home lab.
 Do these models require a subscription? 
 Most offer free apps and services but some advanced features or cloud sync may require a subscription. Check the specific model details for app availability.
